title: How IELTS Writing is marked
bn: What examiners look for and how they give marks
goal: In this chapter you will learn the format of the Writing paper, what the four criteria really ask for, which mistakes cost you marks, and how to split your 60 minutes.

pages.h: The Writing paper at a glance

blocks.x: IELTS Academic Writing has two tasks, and you get 60 minutes in total. There is no separate timer for each task, so you decide how to divide the time yourself. **Time control is in your hands**, so keep this in mind.

head: Task 1
Task 2
rows: A report on a graph, chart, table, map or process diagram
An essay in response to a question
Double, so it has more effect on your final band
Argument, with your own clear position

x: The other three criteria are the same for both tasks: Coherence and Cohesion, Lexical Resource, and Grammatical Range and Accuracy.
In the paper-based test you write by hand on the answer sheet. In the computer-delivered test you type on screen, and the screen shows your word count.
Academic Task 1 never asks for a letter. Letters appear only in General Training.
The question paper says 'Write at least 150 words' or 'at least 250 words'. This is a minimum, not an upper limit.

blocks.x: Aim for 170-190 words in Task 1 and 270-300 words in Task 2. Writing more earns no bonus, but it raises the chance of mistakes and leaves less time to check.
Many students spend 30 minutes on Task 1 and then rush to finish Task 2. Task 2 counts double, so losing time there costs you more.

The examiner gives each task a separate band (0 to 9) for each of the four criteria. The average of these four scores is the band for that task. Task 2 is then given more weight than Task 1 to produce your final Writing band.

A rough formula is (Task 1 + Task 2 + Task 2) / 3. If Task 1 = 7 and Task 2 = 6, you get (7 + 6 + 6) / 3 = 6.33, so your final band will usually be close to 6 or 6.5. The other way round, Task 1 = 6 and Task 2 = 7 gives (6 + 7 + 7) / 3 = 6.67, which is close to 6.5. The numbers are the same, but **a strong Task 2 helps you more**.

x: One very weak criterion pulls the average down. For a 7, all four criteria need to be close to 7.
Grammar and vocabulary are two separate criteria, so about 50% of your marks depend on language.
If your Task Achievement or Task Response is weak, it is hard to get a 7 even with good English.

blocks.q: You get 6.5 in Task 1 and 6 in Task 2. In which task would an extra 0.5 raise your final band more?
blocks.a: Task 2. Task 2 counts double, so an extra 0.5 there adds about 0.33 to your final score. The same gain in Task 1 adds only about 0.17.

pages.h: Criterion 1: Task Achievement and Task Response

blocks.x: This criterion asks one question: did you do exactly what the task asked? In Task 1 it is called Task Achievement (did you report the data accurately?). In Task 2 it is called Task Response (did you answer every part of the question?).

head: Band
Task 1 (Task Achievement) in plain words
Task 2 (Task Response) in plain words
rows: You list the data one item at a time, with no clear overview. Some numbers are wrong or there is very little detail. The answer may be under the word count.
One part of the question is missing. Your position is unclear. There are few ideas, no explanation and a lot of repetition.
There is an overview, but the main features are not well chosen. Some details are irrelevant or wrong.
You touch on every part, but one part is thin. You have a position, but it becomes unclear in the conclusion. Some ideas are not developed.
There is a clear overview that picks out the main trends and differences. The key features are clear but could be developed a little more.
Every part of the question is answered, and your position is clear from start to finish. Main ideas are extended, but some points are too general.
All requirements are well covered. Key features are clearly highlighted, with numbers and comparisons in the right places.
Every part is fully answered. The ideas are relevant, extended and supported with examples or reasons.

x: There is no shortcut to a 7 in Task 1: without an overview, a 7 is almost impossible.
If Task 2 says 'Discuss both views and give your opinion', you need three things: both views and your own opinion.
If you give your own opinion or a reason (for example, why something rose) in Task 1, you lose marks, because the chart does not contain that information.

blocks.x: In Task 2 it is not enough to write about the general topic. If the question is 'Should cars be banned from city centres?' and you only describe the effects of pollution, your answer is on the topic but does not answer the question. At the end of each paragraph, ask yourself: have I answered the question?

blocks.q: A student's Task 1 has every number correct and 200 words, but no overview. Which band will Task Achievement be close to?
blocks.a: Usually around 5. Without an overview, the examiner concludes that you cannot identify the main trends, so the score does not reach 6 even if every number is correct.

blocks.x: Coherence is the logic of your writing: are your ideas in a sensible order, and does each paragraph have one clear focus? Cohesion is how you connect things: linking words, pronouns (this, these, it) and referencing, so the reader can move smoothly from one sentence to the next.

head: Band
In plain words
rows: There is some order, but the text is hard to follow. There are too few linking words, or too many and used wrongly. Paragraphs are not divided properly.
The order is mostly fine. Linkers are used, but mechanically (every sentence starts with 'Firstly', 'Secondly'). In places it is unclear what 'it' or 'this' refers to.
The order is logical and the text is easy to read. There is a range of linkers, though sometimes slightly too many or too few. Each paragraph has one central idea.
Everything is logical and the reader never gets stuck. Linkers are natural and do not draw attention. Paragraphing is correct.

x: Firstly, sales rose. Secondly, they fell. Thirdly, they rose again.
Sales rose at first, then dipped briefly before recovering.
Technology is good. Technology helps students. Technology is cheap.
Technology helps students in two ways. It gives them cheap access to information, and it lets them study at their own pace.
The number of cars increased. The number of cars was 5 million in 2020.
The number of cars increased, reaching 5 million in 2020.

blocks.x: Adding more linkers does not raise your band. It lowers it. If every sentence begins with a linker, the examiner sees the writing as 'mechanical'. Small words such as 'this', 'which' and 'as a result' often do the job.
In Task 2, the first sentence of each body paragraph (the topic sentence) should tell the reader what the paragraph is about. The examiner starts judging coherence from that first line.

Lexical Resource means vocabulary: how wide your range is, whether you use the right word in the right place, whether you know collocations (which words go together), and whether your spelling and word forms are correct.

head: Band
In plain words
rows: Limited words, and the same word again and again. So many spelling mistakes that the text is hard to read.
An adequate range. You try some less common words, but use them wrongly. There are spelling mistakes, but the meaning is still clear.
Flexible and precise. Less common words and collocations are used correctly. Occasional small mistakes.
A wide, natural range. Even rare words are used in the right context. Very few mistakes, mostly in collocation.

x: The price increased very much.
The price rose sharply.
People should do more exercise for good health.
People should take more exercise to stay healthy.
This will make a big problem for the environment.
This will cause serious environmental damage.
The government must make strict rules.
The government must introduce stricter regulations.
Many peoples are economical problem.
Many people face financial difficulties.

blocks.x: Memorising difficult words and forcing them into your writing. A sentence like 'The numbers of cars ameliorated' lowers your band. The examiner wants precise words, not big words. If you are not sure of a word's collocation, do not use it.

blocks.q: Improve this sentence: 'Unemployment is a very big problem and it makes a big effect on young people.'
blocks.a: 'Unemployment is a serious problem, and it has a major effect on young people.' (big problem -> serious problem, makes an effect -> has an effect)

blocks.x: This criterion covers two things: range (a mix of simple, compound and complex sentences) and accuracy (how many sentences are free of errors). Writing complex sentences is not enough. They also need to be error-free.

head: Band
In plain words
rows: Few structures, and mistakes whenever you try a complex sentence. Many errors, including punctuation.
Both simple and complex sentences. There are errors, but they rarely affect the meaning.
A variety of complex structures. Many sentences are completely error-free. A few small errors may remain.
A wide range, and most sentences are error-free. Very few errors.

blocks.x: In the last 3 minutes, look only for your usual mistakes: the -s on verbs, the plural -s, articles (a, an, the) and past tense. Bangladeshi students lose the most marks on these four.

blocks.q: Correct the mistakes: 'Although the price rose, but the sales was increased.'
blocks.a: 'Although the price rose, sales increased.' (Do not use 'although' and 'but' together; 'sales' is plural; 'increase' is intransitive here, so it cannot be passive.)

blocks.x: To the examiner you are a writer, not a memory machine. Anything that shows your real ability is rewarded, and anything that hides it is penalised.

x: What is rewarded: a clear position, an overview, precise vocabulary, error-free complex sentences and logical paragraphs.
You do not need a title. A heading above your essay does not earn extra marks.
Avoid contractions (don't, it's). Write the full forms: do not, it is.
If the examiner cannot read your handwriting, they cannot understand that word, so write neatly in the paper test.

blocks.x: Examiners recognise memorised openings such as 'In this modern era', 'It is a well-known fact that' and 'a double-edged sword' at once. They will not raise your band. They make the examiner doubt the rest of your writing.

blocks.q: A Task 2 essay has 240 words, answers every part, and uses good language. What is the risk?
blocks.a: It is under 250 words, so Task Response is penalised. Losing a band for 10 words makes no sense, so build the habit of writing 270+ words in practice.

blocks.x: You can do the tasks in either order. Most teachers advise writing Task 2 first, because it counts double, and if you run out of time at the end, losing part of Task 1 costs less. On the other hand, starting with Task 1 works as a warm-up. Choose the order you are comfortable with, fix it in practice, and do not change it in the exam.

What to do

Intro 3-4 min, body 1 and body 2 about 10-11 min each, conclusion 3 min
Two points for the overview, grouping for the body
Intro 2 min, overview 3 min, body 9 min

x: Before the exam, do 10 full timed practice tests in a real 60 minutes.
In each practice test, note which part took too long.
Set a checkpoint on the clock: Task 2 must be finished by minute 35.
If you miss a checkpoint, cut down your ideas, but do not stop writing.

blocks.x: In the computer test, copy-paste and the word counter help you, but if your typing is slow, practise first. In the paper test, check whether you write about 10-12 words per line, so you do not need to count every word.
Students often eat into their 3-5 minutes of checking time and keep writing until the last line. Protect both your planning time and your checking time. This is where you can easily save half a band.
If you write without a plan, you run out of ideas halfway and your paragraphs get muddled. A 3-5 minute plan saves you 10 minutes, because you do not have to stop and think while you write.

x: Task 1: check the chart type, the unit (%, millions, tonnes) and the time period.
Task 1: find the two biggest things (the main trend, the highest/lowest, the biggest change). These form your overview.
Task 1: divide the data into two groups. These become your two body paragraphs.
Task 1: circle 4-6 numbers for each body paragraph.

blocks.x: Some people believe that university students should pay the full cost of their studies. Others think that higher education should be free for everyone. Discuss both views and give your own opinion. Write at least 250 words.

x: Instruction words: 'Discuss both views' + 'give your own opinion' = three parts.
Decide your position: I think a basic degree should be free, but with some conditions.
Body 1 (the view that students should pay): graduates earn more, so it is fair for them to bear the cost; it reduces the burden on taxpayers.
Body 2 (the free view + my opinion): poor but talented students are left out; an educated population benefits the country.
Conclusion: restate your opinion, with no new ideas.
Write notes of 3-4 words in your plan, not full sentences.
Next to each idea, write one example or result. This makes the idea easier to develop.
When your plan is finished, read the question again: are all three parts covered?

blocks.q: Task: 'Many cities are banning cars from their centres. Do the advantages of this outweigh the disadvantages?' How many parts does your plan need?
blocks.a: Advantages, disadvantages, and your clear judgement (whether the advantages are greater or smaller). Listing advantages and disadvantages alone does not answer the question.

title: The Task 1 framework
bn: The four-paragraph structure, the overview and choosing data
goal: This chapter teaches you to write any Task 1 chart in four paragraphs, paraphrase the question, build a strong overview and choose the right data.

blocks.x: Every Task 1 chart (line, bar, pie, table, map, process) can be written with the same structure. Once you know this shape by heart, you do not have to think about structure in the exam. You only need to work with the data.

head: Paragraph
What it contains
Sentences
Words
rows: A paraphrase of the question: what it shows, where and when
Details of the first group, with numbers and comparisons
Details of the second group, with numbers and comparisons

blocks.x: The graph below shows the percentage of households with broadband internet access in three countries between 2004 and 2024. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant. Write at least 150 words.

c.title: Households with broadband access in three countries, 2004-2024

x: The line graph compares the proportion of homes with a broadband connection in Canada, Brazil and India over a 20-year period starting in 2004.
Overall, broadband access rose in all three countries. Canada had the highest level of access throughout, while India, which started from almost zero, saw the fastest growth in the final decade.

In 2004, just over a third of Canadian households (35%) had broadband, compared with only 8% in Brazil and a mere 1% in India. Over the next ten years, the Canadian figure more than doubled to 78%, and Brazil's rose to 41%. India, by contrast, made little progress, reaching just 9% by 2014.

From 2014 onwards, growth in Canada slowed as it neared full coverage, with the proportion edging up to 92% by 2024. Brazil continued to climb at a steady pace, ending the period at 74%. The most dramatic change occurred in India, where access tripled to 28% in 2019 and then nearly doubled again to 55% in 2024, although this was still well below the other two countries.
notes: In the intro, 'shows' becomes 'compares', 'percentage of households' becomes 'proportion of homes', and '2004 and 2024' becomes 'a 20-year period starting in 2004'.
The overview has no numbers, only two big points: all countries grew, Canada stayed on top, and India grew fastest.
The body is divided by time: 2004-2014 and 2014-2024. This is an easy grouping for a line graph.
Numbers come with meaning: 'just over a third (35%)', 'more than doubled', 'tripled'. It is not just a list of numbers.
The last line makes a comparison ('still well below'), which meets the Task 1 instruction 'make comparisons'.

blocks.x: Task 1 does not need a separate conclusion paragraph starting with 'In conclusion'. Your overview is your summary. Copying the overview again at the end only wastes words.

The introduction has one job: to say the question in your own words. If you copy the question's sentence, those words are not counted, and the examiner cannot see your vocabulary. Change three things: the verb, the noun phrase and the time phrase.

blocks.x: Changing the data while paraphrasing. Writing 'teenagers' for 'people aged 16-24' is wrong, because people aged 20-24 are not teenagers. Writing 'in the last 20 years' for 'Between 2000 and 2020' is wrong, because you do not know what year the reader is in. Keep categories and years exact.
Do not try to change every word. Keep technical words such as 'broadband', 'rice' and 'engineering' the same. Forcing a synonym can change the meaning.

blocks.q: Paraphrase this: 'The chart below shows the amount of money spent on books by students in four countries in 2022.'
blocks.a: 'The bar chart compares how much students in four countries spent on books in 2022.'

blocks.q: What is wrong with this paraphrase? Question: 'the percentage of adults who smoke'. Student: 'the number of adult smokers'.
blocks.a: A percentage has been turned into a number. A percentage is a proportion, not a number. Write: 'the proportion of adults who smoke'.

blocks.x: The overview is the most valuable paragraph in Task 1. Here you describe the **big picture** of the chart: what stands out when you zoom out. The quality of your overview decides whether Task Achievement gets a 6 or a 7.

x: Main trend: did all the lines go up, go down or stay stable?
Highest and lowest: which category was always at the top, and which was always at the bottom?
Biggest change: what changed the most, and did the order change?
Process: how many stages there are, where it starts and where it ends.
Map: how the area changed overall (more residential, more modern) and what stayed the same.

blocks.x: Do not put numbers in the overview. A specific figure such as '38% in 2020' turns the overview into detail. Numbers belong in the body. Repeating the question with 'Overall, the chart shows...' is not an overview either.

x: Line graph: Overall, the number of cars was 20 million in 2020, which was more than in 2000.
Overall, car ownership increased steadily throughout the period, and petrol cars remained the most common type.
Bar chart: Overall, the chart shows water use in five cities.
Overall, Perth residents used by far the most water, and consumption fell only in Perth and Oslo.
Pie chart: Overall, heating was 52% and 38%.
Overall, heating was the main use of household energy in both years, but appliances showed the biggest rise in share.
Table: Overall, the table has many numbers for rice.
Overall, China produced far more rice than the other three countries, and output rose in every country except Thailand in the final decade.
Process: Overall, first the clay is dug.
Overall, brick production involves eight stages, beginning with digging clay and ending with delivery to customers.
Map: Overall, there are many changes in the village.
Overall, the village became far more developed, with farmland and woodland largely replaced by buildings, although the school remained on its original site.

c.title: Rice production in four countries (million tonnes)

blocks.x: Think of the overview as two points: point 1 = the trend or change, point 2 = the comparison (highest/lowest). You can join them in one or two sentences with 'while' or 'and'.
Write the overview straight after the introduction (paragraph 2). If you leave it to the end and run out of time, the overview gets left out, and without an overview you cannot get a 7.

blocks.q: Write an overview for the cafe line graph (hot coffee fell from 400 to 180, iced coffee rose from 50 to 340, tea stayed stable at around 150).
blocks.a: 'Overall, sales of hot coffee fell steadily while iced coffee became much more popular, overtaking hot coffee by the end of the period. Tea sales, by contrast, hardly changed.'

blocks.x: In Task 1 you do not need to write every number, and if you do, the examiner calls it 'mechanical'. Your job is **selection**: pick the important numbers and arrange them in logical groups so they form two body paragraphs.

c.title: Main reason for visiting a public library, by age group

x: Find the big pattern in the chart: in the library, younger people mostly study, and older people mostly borrow books.
Decide on the grouping: Body 1 = studying and borrowing (opposite trends), Body 2 = using computers (peaks in the middle).
In each group, choose the highest, the lowest and one interesting point.
Leave out the other numbers. Out of 12 numbers, 7-8 are enough.
58% of 16-24 studied, 18% borrowed books and 16% used computers. 22% of 25-44 studied, 41% borrowed books and 27% used computers.
Studying was the main reason for 16-24-year-olds (58%), but this figure fell sharply with age to just 6% among those aged 65 and over.
45-64 borrowing was 47%. 65+ borrowing was 61%.
Borrowing books, by contrast, grew more popular with age, rising from 18% of the youngest group to 61% of the oldest.

blocks.x: Reading the chart one item at a time from left to right is not grouping. The examiner wants to see that you understand the chart, so put similar or opposite things together.

blocks.q: In the library chart, what is special about 'Using computers', and what will you write in the body?
blocks.a: It is highest in the middle age groups: it rises from 16% (16-24) to a peak of 29% (45-64), then drops to 21% among those aged 65+. Write: 'Computer use peaked among 45-64-year-olds at 29%, before falling to 21% in the oldest group.'

blocks.x: Wrong numbers lower your Task Achievement score. But numbers alone make the writing dry. Good writers mix exact numbers with approximations, and they never leave out the unit.

Check the chart title and axis labels for the unit: %, millions, thousands, tonnes, litres. If the unit is 'thousands', 45 means 45,000. Write '45,000 visitors' or '45 thousand visitors'.

blocks.q: Give an approximation for each: 49%, 31%, 76%, 12%.
blocks.a: 49%: just under half. 31%: almost a third. 76%: just over three quarters. 12%: around one in eight.

blocks.q: Unemployment went from 4% to 8%. Why is 'Unemployment increased by 4%' wrong, and what is correct?
blocks.a: A change from 4% to 8% is 4 percentage points, but in proportional terms it is a 100% increase (it doubled). Write: 'The unemployment rate doubled, from 4% to 8%.'

blocks.x: Your tense depends on the time of the data, not on the date of your exam. Use past tense for past years, future forms for future projections, and present tense when there is no time.

blocks.x: The graph below shows the number of people aged 65 and over, and 75 and over, in Japan from 1990 to 2020, with projections to 2040. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant. Write at least 150 words.

c.title: Population aged 65 and over in Japan, 1990-2040 (2030 and 2040 projected)

x: In 2030, the 65+ population rose to 37.2 million.
By 2030, the 65+ population is expected to rise to 37.2 million.
The over-75 group increases from 6 million in 1990 to 18.7 million in 2020.
The over-75 group increased from 6 million in 1990 to 18.7 million in 2020.
In 2040 the over-75 figure will fall slightly to 22.4 million, it is predicted.
The over-75 figure is predicted to dip slightly to 22.4 million in 2040.

blocks.x: Using 'will' again and again with projection data sounds too certain. Mix it up: 'is expected to', 'is projected to', 'is set to', 'is likely to'. Remember to present a projection as a prediction, not a fact.

blocks.q: Write an overview for the Japan graph (mixing past and future).
blocks.a: 'Overall, the elderly population of Japan grew rapidly between 1990 and 2020 and is projected to keep rising, though more slowly. The over-75 group is expected to make up a growing share of older people.'

pages.h: Putting it together: a pie chart answer

blocks.x: The pie charts below show how household energy was used in one country in 1990 and 2020. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant. Write at least 150 words.

c.title: Household energy use by purpose in one country, 1990 and 2020

x: Plan, overview: heating was at the top in both years but fell; appliances grew the most and moved into second place.
Plan, Body 1: the picture in 1990 (heating 52%, water heating 20%, the rest about 10% each).
Plan, Body 2: the changes by 2020 (fell: heating, lighting, water heating; rose: appliances, cooking).
Tense: both years are in the past, so use past simple and past perfect.
The pie charts show how energy consumption in homes in one country was divided among five uses in 1990 and 2020.

Overall, heating was the largest single use of household energy in both years, although its share fell considerably. The most striking change was the rise of appliances, which had become the second biggest category by 2020.

In 1990, heating alone accounted for just over half of all domestic energy use (52%). Water heating came a distant second at 20%, while lighting, appliances and cooking each made up roughly a tenth of the total, at 11%, 9% and 8% respectively.

Thirty years later, the share used for heating had dropped to 38%, and lighting's portion had fallen by almost half to 6%. Water heating also declined slightly, to 18%. In contrast, the proportion consumed by appliances tripled from 9% to 27%, overtaking water heating. Cooking was the only other category to grow, rising modestly from 8% to 11%.
notes: The overview has two features: heating stays on top but falls, and appliances rise sharply. There are no numbers.
Grouping: Body 1 = a snapshot of 1990, Body 2 = what changed by 2020. This is a clear system for pie charts.
Varied language for proportion: accounted for, made up, share, portion, proportion.
Approximation + number: 'just over half (52%)', 'roughly a tenth', 'tripled'.
'respectively' puts three numbers in one sentence without repetition.
The past perfect 'had dropped' and 'had become' shows change up to 2020.

blocks.q: Which sentence in Body 2 of the model makes a comparison, and why does this matter?
blocks.a: '...tripled from 9% to 27%, overtaking water heating.' It compares two categories, which meets the Task 1 instruction 'make comparisons where relevant'.

title: Line graphs

goal: In this chapter you will learn how to pick out the main trends in a line graph, group them sensibly and report them with numbers in a band 8 style.

pages.h: What a line graph is really testing

blocks.x: A line graph is almost always about **change over time**. The examiner wants to see whether you can identify the trends, not whether you can copy every point. You cannot fit 30 numbers into 150 words, so your job is to choose the important points.

First, check the x-axis and the unit. Are the years evenly spaced ('2000, 2005, 2010') or uneven? Is the unit '%', 'millions' or 'TWh'? If you get the unit wrong, your Task Achievement score drops straight away.

You have two body paragraphs. The question is which line goes in which paragraph. The rule is simple: **keep lines that behave in a similar way together**, and show the contrast inside the paragraph.

By time: 2000 to 2010 in one paragraph and 2010 to 2020 in the other (if all the lines change direction at the same time).

By story: if one line is the 'main character' (for example, it overtakes all the others), give it its own paragraph.

blocks.x: If you split paragraphs by year, you will repeat the same item names again and again, and you will not be able to show change. Split by item and keep the years inside your sentences.

blocks.q: A chart shows car ownership in 5 countries in 2010 and 2020. It rose in 3 countries and fell in 2. How would you group them?
blocks.a: Para 1: the 3 countries where it rose (the biggest rise first). Para 2: the 2 countries where it fell. In the overview, write: 'ownership rose in most countries but fell in two'.

pages.h: Walkthrough: exercise by age and sex

blocks.x: The bar chart below shows the percentage of men and women in one country who did regular exercise in 2022, by age group. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant. Write at least 150 words.

c.title: Adults who exercise regularly, by age and sex, 2022

x: There is no time trend, only one year (2022). So use the past tense and comparison language.
Pattern 1: for both sexes, exercise falls with age. Pattern 2: men are well ahead in the young groups, women are slightly ahead after 35, and men are slightly ahead again at 65+.
Biggest gap: 16-24 (58 vs 46 = 12 points). Closest figures: 35-44 (41 vs 42).
Grouping: Para 1 = the decline for men and the gap in the youngest group. Para 2 = the gradual decline for women and where women are ahead.
Chosen numbers: men 58, 49, 36, 24; women 44, 42, 38/33, 22. You do not need all 12.
The bar chart compares the percentages of men and women in one country who exercised regularly in 2022, broken down into six age groups.

Overall, participation in regular exercise fell steadily with age for both sexes. Men were noticeably more active than women in the two youngest groups, but this pattern was reversed in middle age, and the figures for the two sexes were broadly similar from the age of 35 onwards.

Among 16 to 24-year-olds, 58% of men exercised regularly, compared with 46% of women, the widest gap on the chart. For men, the figure dropped with each older age group, to 49% for those aged 25 to 34 and 36% for the 45 to 54 group, before falling to just 24% among the over-65s.

The decline for women was much more gradual. Their rate stood at 44% in the 25 to 34 group and 42% in the 35 to 44 group, slightly above the male figure of 41%. Women remained marginally ahead in the next two groups as well (38% and 33%, against 36% and 30% for men). In the oldest group, however, men were again slightly more active, at 24% compared with 22%.
notes: 'fell with age' describes a trend-like pattern on a comparison chart, without wrong time language such as 'increased in 2022'.
The overview combines 3 ideas: decline with age, men ahead when young, and similar figures later.
'the widest gap on the chart' highlights an important feature.
The numbers in brackets '(38% and 33%, against 36% and 30%)' save words and stay accurate.
'marginally', 'noticeably' and 'slightly' state the size of each difference precisely.

blocks.x: For age groups, write '16 to 24-year-olds' or 'those aged 16 to 24' instead of '16-24'. This is natural English, and it avoids any confusion over the dash or hyphen in a range.

pages.h: Full task: family spending over time

blocks.x: The chart below shows the average weekly amount spent by families in one country on four items in 1980, 2000 and 2020. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant. Write at least 150 words.

c.title: Average weekly family spending on four items
x: Food
Housing
Transport
Entertainment

blocks.x: This chart has time in it (3 years), so you need trend language. Still, split the paragraphs by item, not by year: Para 1 = housing and food (the big items), Para 2 = transport and entertainment (the smaller items).

x: The bar chart shows how much an average family in one country spent each week on food, housing, transport and entertainment in 1980, 2000 and 2020.

Overall, spending on all four categories increased over the forty years. Housing was the largest expense in every year and also saw the biggest rise, while entertainment, though still the smallest item, grew at the fastest rate.

In 1980, a typical family spent $60 a week on housing and $45 on food, compared with only $20 on transport and $10 on entertainment. By 2000, housing costs had risen to $95, and by 2020 they had reached $150, two and a half times the 1980 figure. Food spending, in contrast, grew relatively slowly, from $45 to $55 and then to $62.

Transport costs almost doubled between 1980 and 2000, from $20 to $38, but rose only modestly after that, to $45 in 2020. Entertainment showed the most dramatic change: weekly spending more than doubled to $22 in 2000 and then nearly doubled again to $41, so that by 2020 it was not far behind transport.
notes: The overview separates the 'biggest rise' (absolute) from the 'fastest rate' (proportional). This is clever analysis.
'By 2000, housing costs had risen' uses the past perfect, which sounds natural with 'by + year'.
'two and a half times the 1980 figure' is worked out: 150 / 60 = 2.5.
The grouping is by item, so the full story of each item is in one place.
The last line ends the comparison by mentioning the closing gap between entertainment and transport.

blocks.x: For money, write '$60', not '60$'. Mention the unit 'dollars' once in the intro.

pages.h: Full task: reasons for choosing a course

blocks.x: The chart below shows the main reasons undergraduate and postgraduate students at one university gave for choosing their course. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant. Write at least 150 words.

c.title: Main reason for choosing a course
x: Career prospects
Personal interest
Family advice
Course reputation
Location

blocks.x: This is a horizontal chart with no time and no year. So which tense? The survey took place in the past, so the past tense is safe. Grouping: Para 1 = the top 2 reasons (same order in both groups), Para 2 = where the difference is larger (family advice) and the smaller reasons.

x: The bar chart compares the main reasons undergraduate and postgraduate students at a university gave for choosing their course.

Overall, career prospects were the most common reason in both groups, followed by personal interest. The biggest difference between the two groups concerned family advice, which mattered far more to undergraduates than to postgraduates.

Just over half of postgraduates (52%) said they had chosen their course mainly for career reasons, compared with 38% of undergraduates. Personal interest came second for both groups, with similar figures of 30% for postgraduates and 27% for undergraduates.

The two groups differed sharply on the role of family advice. This was the main reason for 18% of undergraduates, making it their third most important factor, but for only 4% of postgraduates, the lowest figure for that group. The remaining reasons were relatively minor for both groups. Course reputation was mentioned by 11% of undergraduates and 9% of postgraduates, while location was the least common reason among undergraduates (6%) and was cited by a similar 5% of postgraduates.
notes: A fraction plus a number, as in 'Just over half (52%)', is precise and natural.
Ranking language ('came second', 'third most important', 'the lowest figure') is ideal for a comparison chart.
The first sentence of Body 2 is a topic sentence. It tells the reader what the paragraph is about.
The reporting verbs vary ('mentioned', 'cited', 'said') without straining for synonyms.
All 10 numbers are included, but each one sits inside a comparison, not in a list.

blocks.q: 'Career prospects was the most popular reason for 52% of postgraduates.' What is the problem?
blocks.a: Using 'most popular' and '52%' together is redundant and a little awkward. Better: 'Career prospects were the main reason for 52% of postgraduates, the most common answer in that group.'

blocks.x: Misreading bar values. Line each bar up with the gridlines before you read it. If you are unsure, write 'about 40%', not a made-up exact figure such as '43%'.
Mixing up the legend. Check twice which colour is men and which is women before you write. If you put numbers on the wrong series, the whole paragraph is wrong.
Adding things that are not on the chart: 'Young men exercise more because they play football.' Giving explanations lowers your Task Achievement score.
Using the same sentence pattern for every category: 'The figure for X was A. The figure for Y was B.' Vary the structure with compared with, while, followed by and brackets.

Does the overview include the highest/lowest or the main pattern?
Is the grouping by category or pattern, and not just by series?
Does every paragraph compare, and not just describe?
Have you used the right noun: 'number', 'amount' or 'proportion'?
Are the units ($, %, thousands) right everywhere?

blocks.q: A bar chart shows the number of tourists in 6 countries in 2015 and 2020. What should you look for to write the overview?
blocks.a: 1) Whether the number rose or fell in most countries, 2) which country stayed at the top throughout, 3) whether any country changed its ranking. Pick 2 of these points for the overview.

title: Pie charts
bn: Smart comparison with shares, proportions and fractions
goal: In this chapter you will learn to pick out the main shares from one or two pie charts, use fraction language, and report changes accurately.

blocks.x: All the slices in a pie chart add up to 100%. So the language of pie charts is the language of **share**: 'accounted for', 'made up', 'took up', 'the proportion of'. You do not know the absolute numbers. You only know the proportions.

The same, but in the past tense

blocks.x: Two pies from two different years really show 'change over time', so you can use trend verbs (rose, fell). These verbs apply to the **share**: 'the share of housing rose from 22% to 33%'.
If a pie has many slices (6 or more), group the small ones together: 'The remaining three categories together made up just 17%.'

Getting the direction wrong, as in 'Food rose from 38% to 21%', or writing 'food spending fell' when only the share fell. If the total budget grows, the money spent on food can rise while its share falls. So write 'the proportion spent on food fell'.
With two pies, the most common mistake is Para 1 = the 1990 pie and Para 2 = the 2020 pie. This gives no comparison, and the reader has to compare the figures alone. Group by category instead.

The big slices (the top 2 or 3) in one paragraph, the small slices in the other.
The slices whose ranking changed in one paragraph.
For a single pie: the largest group in one paragraph, the smaller group in the other.

blocks.a: Para 1: coal and nuclear (both fell), and the top position passing from coal to gas. Para 2: gas and solar (both rose), solar growing six times over, and 'other' unchanged in one line.

blocks.x: The pie charts below show how the average household in one country spent its income in 1990 and 2020. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant. Write at least 150 words.

c.title: Household spending by category

x: Two years, so use the past tense and the language of change.
Biggest feature: food and housing swap places (from 38 vs 22 to 21 vs 33).
Second feature: transport, healthcare and education all rose; 'other' fell.
Calculations: food 21 / 38 = 0.55, which means 'little more than half'. Healthcare 6 to 11, 'almost doubled'. Housing + food: from 60% to 54%.
Grouping: Body 1 = food and housing. Body 2 = the other four.
The pie charts compare how the average household in one country divided its spending between six categories in 1990 and 2020.

Overall, the pattern of spending changed considerably over the 30 years. Food, the largest item in 1990, lost its top position to housing, while the shares spent on transport, healthcare and education all increased.

In 1990, food took up 38% of household budgets, well ahead of housing at 22%. By 2020, these positions had been reversed: housing accounted for a third of spending (33%), while the proportion going on food had fallen to 21%, little more than half its earlier level. Taken together, these two essentials made up 60% of spending in 1990 but 54% in 2020.

The three service categories each took a larger share by the end of the period. Transport rose from 10% to 15% and education from 9% to 12%, while healthcare almost doubled, from 6% to 11%. The only other category to shrink was miscellaneous spending, labelled 'other', which dropped from 15% to just 8%.
notes: In the overview, 'lost its top position to housing' states the ranking change in one line.
'little more than half its earlier level' is worked out from the figures. Examiners see this as strong data analysis.
The 'Taken together' sentence adds two slices to make a new point, rather than copying the chart.
'took up', 'accounted for' and 'made up' vary the share verb while the meaning stays the same.
The small slices are compressed into one sentence with 'Transport rose ... and education ...'.

pages.h: Full task: student travel to university

blocks.x: The pie charts below show the main methods of transport used by students to travel to a university in 2005 and 2025. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant. Write at least 150 words.

c.title: How students travel to the university

blocks.x: Plan: Body 1 = a brief look at the 2005 ranking. Body 2 = the changes by 2025: the car's share fell by more than half, the bus moved to the top and cycling tripled. Grouping by year works for this chart, because every change in Body 2 is compared with its 2005 figure.

x: The two pie charts show how students travelled to a university in 2005 and 2025.

Overall, there was a clear shift away from the car towards other forms of transport. The car was the most common way of getting to the university in 2005, but by 2025 the bus had taken first place and cycling had become far more popular.
In 2005, 41% of students travelled by car, considerably more than the 26% who took the bus. Walking was the third most common method (16%), followed by cycling (9%) and the train (8%).

Twenty years later, the share of students driving had fallen by more than half, to 18%. The bus became the most popular option, although its share rose only slightly, to 30%. The most dramatic increase was in cycling, which almost tripled from 9% to 24%, making it the second most common method. The train also gained ground, rising to 13%, while the proportion of students walking remained almost unchanged at 15%.
notes: In the overview, 'shift away from the car' gives a clear direction.
'by 2025 the bus had taken first place' is a good use of the past perfect.
'although its share rose only slightly' keeps the reason for the bus reaching the top accurate: the bus did not grow much, it reached the top because car use fell.
The calculations for 'almost tripled' (9 to 24) and 'fallen by more than half' (41 to 18) are correct.
Ranking language ('third most common', 'second most common') is the natural language of pie charts.

blocks.x: The two pies may not show the slices in the same order. Match slices by their labels, not by colour or position.

pages.h: Full task: a single pie with no time

blocks.x: The pie chart below shows how water is used in an average home in one city. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant. Write at least 150 words.

c.title: Household water use in one city

blocks.x: There is no year here, so use the **present simple**. Trend verbs (rose, fell) do not work at all. Just compare: largest, smallest, combined shares and ratios.

x: The pie chart shows how water is used in an average home in one city, divided into seven categories.

The most noticeable feature is that personal washing and toilet flushing together account for well over half of all household water use. By contrast, appliances in the kitchen and water used outside the home make up only small shares.

Showers and baths are the largest single use, at 32%, closely followed by toilets at 27%. Combined, these two categories represent almost three fifths (59%) of the total. The washing machine is responsible for 13% of consumption, which is slightly more than the 11% that comes from the kitchen tap.

The remaining three categories are relatively minor. Watering the garden takes up 8% of household water, while miscellaneous uses, grouped as 'other', account for 5%. The dishwasher uses the least water of all, just 4%, which is roughly a third of the share used by the kitchen tap and one eighth of that used for showers and baths.
notes: The overview opens with 'The most noticeable feature is' instead of 'Overall', for variety.
The present simple is used consistently throughout, because the chart has no year.
'Combined, ... (59%)' adds slices together to make a new point.
Ratios ('roughly a third', 'one eighth') link the small slices to the big ones.
The topic sentence of Body 2, 'The remaining three categories are relatively minor', organises the paragraph.

blocks.q: How do you write an overview for a single pie when there is no trend?
blocks.a: State the largest category or the largest group of categories, and add a contrast: 'X and Y dominate, while the remaining categories each account for less than 15%.'

blocks.x: Describing the two pies in separate paragraphs. Try to include both 1990 and 2020 in each sentence: 'from A to B'.
Writing 'increased by 5%' when a share went from 10% to 15%. That is 5 percentage points, which is a 50% increase. The simple way out: 'rose from 10% to 15%'.
Mixing present and past. Use the past if there is a year and the present if there is not, and keep it consistent through the whole answer.
If the slice percentages do not add up to 100, you have misread something. Add up the numbers to check.

x: Have you used share language (accounted for, made up, the proportion of)?
Is it clear what each percentage refers to (of students, of income)?
With two pies, have you compared by category and not pie by pie?
Have you used at least two fraction phrases (a third, just over half)?
Have you grouped the small slices to save words?
Does the overview include a ranking change or the largest share?

blocks.q: Correct this: 'In 2025, bicycle was increased to 24%.'
blocks.a: 'By 2025, the share of students cycling had increased to 24%.' Drop the passive. Also, the bicycle itself did not increase; the share did.

title: Tables
bn: Finding the pattern in a mass of numbers
goal: This chapter teaches you to find patterns in a table for yourself, group the data sensibly by row or column, and report a lot of data selectively.

blocks.x: With a line graph or a bar chart, you can see the trend at a glance. A table gives you no picture, so **you have to find the pattern yourself**. That is why tables need more planning time: 3 to 4 minutes.

x: Read the unit and the title: thousands? millions? %? Different columns may use different units.
Circle the highest and lowest values in each column.
Check the direction of each row: rising, falling, or up then down?
Does one row or column behave differently from the rest? That is your standout feature.
Do some calculations: what has doubled, which rankings have changed, what the totals are.

blocks.x: On the question paper, draw small arrows (up, down, flat) next to the table in pencil. In 30 seconds you will see every trend in the table.
Reporting every number in the table. If there are 15 cells and you write 15 numbers, you get a list and lose the overview. Choosing 8 to 12 important numbers is enough.
A table gives you 3 options for grouping: by row, by column or by pattern. Grouping by pattern works best, because the examiner wants analysis.

Grouping idea

By measure: Para 1 = age and size, Para 2 = passengers

Do not give every number in a row. Give the start, the end and one interesting point.
If columns use different units (km, millions), put each one in a separate sentence. Do not mix them.

blocks.q: A table shows life expectancy in 6 countries in 2000 and 2020. It rose by 3 to 8 years in 5 countries and fell by 2 years in one. What is the overview?
blocks.a: 'Overall, life expectancy rose in five of the six countries, with [country] the only one to see a decline.' Then mention the highest and lowest countries.

blocks.x: The table below shows the number of international students studying in five countries in 2010, 2015 and 2020. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant. Write at least 150 words.

c.title: International students, by host country (thousands)

x: Unit: thousands. So 690 means 690,000. Write '690,000' in your answer.
Arrows: USA up then down; UK up, up; Australia up, up; Canada up, up; Japan up, up.
Standout: the USA is the only country whose figure fell in 2020, yet it stays at the top. Canada grows fastest: from 100 to 320, more than tripling.
Australia: from 230 to 460, exactly double. Canada overtakes Japan in 2015 (170 vs 150).

The table gives the number of international students in five countries in 2010, 2015 and 2020, in thousands.

Overall, the USA hosted by far the most international students in all three years. Every country except the USA saw continuous growth, and the most rapid expansion was in Canada, where student numbers more than tripled.

The USA's total rose sharply from 690,000 in 2010 to 970,000 in 2015, before falling slightly to 910,000 in 2020. Even after this decline, it remained well ahead of the UK, the second most popular destination, which had 550,000 international students in 2020. The UK's figure had changed little between 2010 and 2015 (410,000 and 430,000) before rising more noticeably in the following five years.

Among the three smaller destinations, Australia doubled its intake, from 230,000 to 460,000. Canada had the lowest number in 2010, at 100,000, but it overtook Japan by 2015 and reached 320,000 in 2020. Japan's growth was slower: its figure rose only slightly, from 140,000 to 150,000, in the first five years and then increased to 230,000.

The overview has two clear features: the exception ('Every country except the USA') and the fastest growth.
'Even after this decline, it remained well ahead' links the USA and the UK in a comparison sentence.
Para 2 opens with 'Among the three smaller destinations', which makes the grouping clear to the reader.
'doubled', 'more than tripled' and 'overtook' are insights worked out from the table. They are not written in it.
14 of the 15 numbers are used, but every one sits inside a comparison, not in a list.

head: City

x: The table compares the underground railway systems of five cities in terms of the year they opened, the length of their routes and the number of passengers they carry each year.

Overall, Tokyo's system is the busiest by a wide margin, although Delhi has the longest network. The two newest systems differ greatly: Delhi's is already among the largest, whereas Lima's is the smallest on every measure.

Paris has the oldest metro, opened in 1900, followed by Tokyo in 1927. Despite this, neither has the most extensive network. Delhi's system, which opened as recently as 2002, has 393 km of route, compared with 304 km in Tokyo and 226 km in Paris.

In terms of passengers, Tokyo carries 3,200 million people a year, more than double the figure for Paris (1,500 million) and considerably more than Delhi (1,950 million). The overview gives the winners on two different measures (busiest vs longest) and the contrast with the newer systems.

pages.h: Full task: social media use by age

blocks.x: The table below shows the percentage of people in different age groups who used five types of social media every day in 2024. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant. Write at least 150 words.

c.title: Daily use of social media types by age group, 2024 (%)

blocks.x: Arrows: 4 of the rows fall from left to right (use drops as age rises). The professional networking row is different: 18, 39, 27, 4, with a peak in the middle. This is your exception, and it goes in the overview.

x: The table shows the percentages of people in four age groups who used five types of social media every day in 2024.

Overall, messaging apps were the most widely used platform in every age group, and daily use of almost all types of social media declined as age increased. Professional networking was the only exception, as it was most popular among people aged 25 to 44.

Messaging apps were used daily by 94% of 16 to 24-year-olds and 91% of 25 to 44-year-olds. Use remained high in the 45 to 64 group (83%), and even among the over-65s the figure was 61%, more than double that of any other platform for that age group. Video sharing followed a similar but steeper pattern, falling from 89% of the youngest users to 28% of the oldest.

The sharpest age difference was in photo sharing, which was used daily by 72% of the youngest group but by just 7% of those aged 65 and over. Online forums were less popular overall, with figures ranging from 31% down to 6%. Professional networking, meanwhile, was used by 39% of 25 to 44-year-olds, compared with 27% of 45 to 64-year-olds, 18% of the youngest group and only 4% of the oldest.
notes: The overview gives a general rule plus an exception, which is the ideal formula for a table.
'more than double that of any other platform for that age group' (61 vs 28) is a comparison within a column.
'a similar but steeper pattern' links two rows instead of describing each one separately.
The age groups are varied as 'the over-65s' and 'the youngest group', which cuts down repetition.
The exception (professional networking) comes last, so the paragraph ends on a clear point.

blocks.q: Is it right to use the word 'declined' in this table when there is no time?
blocks.a: 'declined as age increased' is fine, because you are describing a pattern across age groups, not a change over time. But 'declined in 2024' is wrong, because nothing can decline within a single year.

blocks.x: Forgetting the unit: if the table says 'thousands', writing '690 students' gets the data wrong. Check the unit in both the title and the column headers.
Writing row by row: 'The USA ... The UK ... Australia ...', which gives five mini paragraphs. Group the rows and compare them instead.
Giving only the highest number in the overview: 'The USA had the highest number.' That is a detail. The overview needs a general pattern plus an exception.
Mixing numbers from different columns: 'Delhi has 393 and 1,950.' Give the unit and the meaning with each number.

x: Did you spend 3 to 4 minutes planning, with arrows and circles?
Does the overview include a general pattern and one exception?
Is the grouping by row, column or pattern logical?
Have you included insights you worked out (doubled, overtook, more than twice)?
Are the units and tenses right?
Have you used 8 to 14 numbers, all inside comparisons?

blocks.q: A table shows sales at 4 shops from January to April. Shop A is top every month, Shop D is last every month, and B and C cross in March. Write the overview.
blocks.a: 'Overall, Shop A recorded the highest sales throughout the period and Shop D the lowest, while Shops B and C changed places in March.'

title: Mixed charts (two visuals)
bn: Two charts, one answer: learn to balance and link them
goal: In this chapter you will learn how to write about two different visuals in one balanced answer, put the main point of each into a single overview, and link the two charts where you can.

blocks.x: A mixed task has two visuals: line + pie, bar + table, pie + table and so on. The word limit stays the same, though: **at least 150 words, 20 minutes**. So you have less time and fewer words for each chart. Selection matters more here than anywhere else.

x: The two charts share a topic, but the data is different (for example, visitor numbers + purpose of visit).
The examiner checks whether you have covered both charts. If you skip one, Task Achievement can drop below 5.
The overview must include the main point of both charts.
If there is a real connection between the two charts (same city, same year), link them in one sentence.

Rain and temperature together: 'the wettest months are also the warmest at night'

If the categories are the same, compare them: 'X was highest in both charts'

Writing the two charts as two mini essays, each with its own overview. There should be only one overview, after the intro, combining the main points of both charts.

Find 1 main feature in each chart. These two go in the overview.
Put the more complex chart in Body 1.
See whether a link is possible: same year, same place?
Check your word count after writing, because answers on two charts tend to run long.

blocks.q: A task has a bar chart (car production in 5 countries, 2010 vs 2020) + a pie chart (car types in 2020: petrol, diesel, electric, hybrid). Write the intro sentence.
blocks.a: 'The bar chart compares car production in five countries in 2010 and 2020, while the pie chart shows the types of car produced in 2020.'

pages.h: Walkthrough: tourism line graph and pie chart

blocks.x: The line graph below shows the number of visitors from Asia and Europe to one country between 2000 and 2020, and the pie chart shows the main purposes of visits in 2019. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant. Write at least 150 words.

charts.title: Visitors from Asia and Europe, 2000 to 2020

x: Line: Europe is higher at first (2.7 vs 1.5), the two are level in 2010 (3.4), then Asia grows fast and peaks at 7.3 in 2019, and both crash in 2020.
Pie: holidays 54%, all the others much smaller.
Overview: growth in both regions (faster in Asia) + the 2020 collapse; holidays made up more than half in 2019.
Link: the pie is for 2019, the peak year on the line graph. You can connect them with 'the year before this fall'.
Body 1 = the line graph (more data). Body 2 = the pie.
The line graph shows how many visitors from Asia and Europe travelled to one country between 2000 and 2020, while the pie chart breaks down the reasons for visiting in 2019.

Overall, visitor numbers from both regions grew for most of the period, with Asian arrivals rising much faster, before both collapsed in 2020. In 2019, the year before this fall, more than half of all visits were holidays.

In 2000, Europe was the larger source of visitors, with 2.7 million arrivals compared with 1.5 million from Asia. The two figures were level at 3.4 million in 2010, after which Asian arrivals increased rapidly, reaching a peak of 7.3 million in 2019. European numbers also rose, but more slowly, to 4.5 million in the same year. In 2020, however, both figures dropped dramatically, to 1.9 million for Asia and just 1.2 million for Europe.

As for the purpose of visits in 2019, holidays accounted for 54% of trips, more than double the share for visiting friends and relatives (21%). Business travel made up 15%, while study and other reasons were much less common, at 6% and 4% respectively.
notes: The intro covers both charts in one sentence, joined with 'while'.
The overview links the two charts with 'the year before this fall'. This is a band 8 move in a mixed task.
The crossing point on the line ('level at 3.4 million in 2010') and the peak are accurate.
'As for' gives a smooth transition to the second chart in Body 2.
The small slices of the pie are covered in one sentence with 'respectively', which saves words.
The units differ between the charts (millions vs %), and both are reported correctly.

blocks.x: Easy phrases to open Body 2 in a mixed task: 'As for ...', 'Turning to ...', 'Regarding ...'. Use one of them; you do not need a different one each time.

The first chart ..., and the second gives a breakdown of ...
Turning to the pie chart, ...
As for the table, ...
This was also the year in which ... (link with the second chart)
The wettest months, which are shown in the bar chart, also have the highest minimum temperatures.
The first chart is about tourists. The second chart is about purpose.

Overall, tourists increased. Overall, holiday is the biggest.
Overall, visitor numbers rose for most of the period, and holidays were by far the main reason for visiting.
Now I will describe the pie chart.
Turning to the pie chart, holidays accounted for more than half of all trips.
Because tourists increased, the country made more business.
(Delete: the charts do not show causes.)
The rain is high in July and the temperature is 31.
July is the wettest month, with 390 mm of rain, while daytime temperatures ease slightly to 31 degrees.

blocks.x: Signposting such as 'Now I will describe ...' or 'Firstly, I will talk about ...' is awkward in an academic report. Start directly with the content of the chart.

blocks.q: Join the two overview sentences into one: 'Spending on salaries was the largest. Student numbers rose in most faculties.'
blocks.a: 'Overall, staff salaries took up the largest share of spending, and student numbers grew in four of the five faculties.'
