blocks.x: 12 months x 3 data sets = 36 numbers! Covering all of them would take 400 words. Choose only the turning points: the driest month, the wettest month, when the rain starts and ends, the hottest month, the coolest month, and where the gap between day and night is smallest. Climate data is a 'general fact', so use the present simple.

x: The charts give information about the climate of a South Asian city, showing average rainfall and average maximum and minimum temperatures for each month of the year.

Overall, the city has a long wet season from May to September and a short, dry and cool period in winter. Rainfall and minimum temperatures follow a broadly similar pattern, while maximum temperatures peak before the heaviest rain arrives.

Rainfall is very low between November and February, ranging from just 8 mm in January to 30 mm in November. It then rises sharply, from 55 mm in March to 280 mm in May, and peaks at 390 mm in July. Levels remain high in August and September (320 mm and 290 mm) before dropping to 160 mm in October.

January is the coolest month, with temperatures between 13 and 25 degrees Celsius. Maximum temperatures climb to a high of 34 degrees in April and May and then ease slightly to around 31 to 32 degrees during the rainy months. Minimum temperatures, by contrast, keep rising until June and stay at 26 degrees until September, so the gap between day and night temperatures is narrowest in the wet season. Both figures fall again from October onwards.
notes: The present simple is used throughout, because a climate average is a general fact.
The overview shows the relationship between the two charts: 'maximum temperatures peak before the heaviest rain arrives'. This is a real link.
Only about 20 of the 36 numbers are chosen, all of them turning points.
'ranging from ... to ...' covers four months in one sentence.
'the gap between day and night temperatures is narrowest in the wet season' is an insight worked out from the data (12 degrees in January, 5 in July).
'ease slightly', 'keep rising' and 'stay at' give variety for small changes.

blocks.x: If the degree symbol is hard to type, write 'degrees Celsius' or '34C'. On computer-delivered IELTS, writing 'degrees' is the safest choice.

pages.h: Full task: university budget and student numbers

blocks.x: The pie chart below shows how a university spent its budget in 2024, and the table shows the number of students in each faculty in 2014 and 2024. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant. Write at least 150 words.
There is no direct link between these two charts (budget breakdown vs student numbers), so do not force one. Give two separate main points in the overview and two separate paragraphs in the body.

x: The pie chart shows how a university divided its budget in 2024, and the table compares the number of students in its five faculties in 2014 and 2024.

Overall, more than half of the university's spending went on staff salaries. Over the ten-year period, total student numbers increased, with growth in every faculty except Arts, and Engineering remained the largest faculty.

Staff salaries made up 52% of the budget in 2024, almost three times as much as the second largest item, buildings and maintenance (18%). Research accounted for 12% of spending and library and IT services for 9%, while student services and other costs received only 6% and 3% respectively.

Turning to enrolment, the total number of students rose from 11,500 in 2014 to 13,400 in 2024. Engineering grew from 3,200 to 4,100 students, but the largest increase was in Business, which gained 1,100 students to reach 3,900. Science and Medicine also expanded, to 2,600 and 1,100 respectively. Arts was the only faculty to shrink, falling from 2,500 students, the third highest figure in 2014, to 1,700, which placed it fourth by 2024.
notes: The overview includes the main point of the pie (salaries over half) and the main point of the table (growth everywhere except Arts).
The calculation for 'almost three times as much as': 52 / 18 = 2.9.
The 'Total' row of the table is used to give the overall change in one sentence.
'the largest increase was in Business' comes from comparing the absolute changes (plus 1,100 vs plus 900 for Engineering).
The answer mentions the change in ranking for Arts (from third to fourth), which you have to work out from the table yourself.
There is no invented link between the two charts. This is accurate Task Achievement.

blocks.q: What is wrong with this sentence: 'Because salaries were 52%, the Arts faculty became smaller.'
blocks.a: The charts show no causes. Report the two facts separately and do not add a cause-and-effect link of your own.

blocks.x: Writing 150 words on one chart and 20 on the other. Keep a balance: the complex chart gets more words, but both must be covered properly.
Two overviews, one before Body 1 and one before Body 2. Write one overview in one place, combining the points from both charts.
Mixing up units: the line uses millions and the pie uses %. Writing '54 million holidays' is wrong. Give each number the unit from its own chart.
Tense mismatch: the line graph is in the past (2000 to 2020), while the climate chart is in the present (general fact). Follow the logic of each chart.

x: Have you paraphrased both charts in the intro?
Is there one overview, with the main point of each chart?
Is there a separate body paragraph for each chart?
Have you mentioned a real link if there is one, and avoided invented links?
Are the unit and tense right for each chart?
Is the total 170 to 210 words, written within 20 minutes?

blocks.q: How should you split the 20 minutes in a mixed task?
blocks.a: 3 to 4 minutes: read both charts and mark the main features. 2 minutes: plan the intro and the overview. 12 minutes: write. 2 minutes: check units, numbers and tenses.

title: Process diagrams
bn: Charts without numbers: a complete system for describing a process stage by stage
goal: In this chapter you will learn how to read natural and man-made process diagrams, count the stages, and write a band 7+ answer with passive verbs and clear sequencing language.

blocks.x: A process diagram has no numbers or percentages. Instead, it uses pictures and arrows to show, stage by stage, how something is made (man-made) or how something happens in nature (natural). Your job is to report every stage in the correct order, using **clear passive and sequencing language**.

head: Type
Typical examples
Main verb form
rows: making bricks, producing tea, recycling glass bottles, making instant noodles
Mostly passive: 'the clay is dug up', 'the bottles are crushed'
how a solar water heater works, how electricity is generated from waves
life cycle of a frog, silkworm or salmon
Mostly active: 'the eggs hatch', 'the larva grows'
the water cycle, formation of sedimentary rock

blocks.x: The other division is linear versus cycle. A linear process has a clear start and a clear end, for example from raw material to finished product. In a cycle, the last stage leads back to the first one, as in the life cycle of a frog or the water cycle.

x: Arrows: they show you the order, but sometimes they branch into two paths.
Labels: these matter most. The words in each label give you the content of your sentences.
Small details: times (24 hours), temperatures (1,000 C) and equipment (conveyor belt). Mentioning them makes your answer more accurate.
Pictures without labels: look at the picture and choose a simple verb, but do not guess if you are unsure.

blocks.x: In your head, turn each label into a full passive sentence. 'Clay dug' becomes 'The clay is dug up from the ground'. Once this becomes a habit, you will write much faster.

Do not add explanations that are not in the diagram. A reason such as 'The leaves are dried because moisture makes them rot' does not belong in Task 1. The examiner only checks whether you have reported the diagram correctly.

pages.h: Counting stages and planning in 3 minutes

blocks.x: Spend 3 minutes planning before you write. The most common mistakes in process answers are missing a stage or putting stages in the wrong order, so never skip the plan.

x: Find the start and the end: where the process begins, where it finishes, or where a cycle returns to the beginning.
Count the stages: each box, or each picture with a label, is one stage. If the process branches, count the stages on each path separately.
Underline numbers, times and temperatures. You need to mention these in the body.
Split the process into two halves at a natural break, for example when the raw material is ready or when the product is finished.
Choose your verb form: passive for man-made processes, mostly active present simple for natural ones.

head: Total stages
Body paragraph 1
Body paragraph 2
rows: Later life and return to start (5 to 7)

blocks.x: If you are not sure how many stages there are, do not give an exact number. Writing 'The process involves a number of distinct stages' instead of 'The process consists of eight stages' still gives you a sound overview.
If two pictures share one label, they form one stage. If one box contains two actions ('washed and dried'), count it as one stage, but use two verbs when you describe it in the body.

blocks.q: A diagram shows: clay dug up, clay sieved, mixed with water and sand, moulded into bricks, dried for 24-48 hours, fired in a kiln, cooled, packed, delivered. How many stages, and where would you split the body?
blocks.a: Nine stages. A good split is after 'dried for 24-48 hours' (the raw brick is ready) or after 'fired in a kiln'. Paragraph 1: digging to drying. Paragraph 2: firing, cooling, packing and delivery.

pages.h: Passive voice: the engine of a process answer

blocks.x: In a man-made process, it does not matter who does the work (a worker or a machine). What matters is the action itself. That is why you use the passive: 'The leaves are picked', 'The mixture is heated'. The present simple passive works throughout, because the process is a general fact.

head: Form
Example
Use it for
rows: The clay is mixed with sand.
The bricks are then placed in a kiln.
The bottles can be reused up to 20 times.
After being dried, the bricks are fired.
Joining two stages in one sentence
Having been cooled, the bricks are packed.
...a conveyor belt, which is powered by a motor.

x: Workers pick the leaves by hand.
The leaves are picked by hand.
A machine rolls them.
They are then rolled by machine.
They put the bricks in a kiln and heat them.
The bricks are placed in a kiln, where they are heated to 1,000 C.
Trucks take the boxes to shops.
Finally, the boxes are transported to shops by lorry.
They dry the bricks. Then they fire the bricks.
After being dried, the bricks are fired.

blocks.x: In natural processes, many verbs are intransitive, which means they take no object: hatch, grow, evaporate, flow, emerge. These verbs cannot be passive. 'The eggs are hatched' is wrong. Write 'The eggs hatch'.

Common mistakes among Bangladeshi students: 'It is happened', and 'The leaves are dry' (an adjective) when you mean 'are dried' (part of the process). Another one is 'are dried by heated', which is wrong. Write 'are dried with hot air' or 'are heated'.

blocks.q: Make these passive: (a) They wash the bottles. (b) A machine crushes the glass. (c) They melt the glass at 1,500 C.
blocks.a: (a) The bottles are washed. (b) The glass is crushed by a machine. (c) The glass is melted at 1,500 C.

blocks.q: Active or passive? 'The young salmon ___ (swim) downstream to the sea.'
blocks.a: Active: 'The young salmon swim downstream to the sea.' Swim is intransitive, so passive is impossible.

blocks.x: If you write 'Then... then... then', it is hard to score above band 6 in Coherence and Cohesion. Use a range of linkers, but make sure each one has the right meaning.

head: Position
Useful language
rows: The process begins with... / In the first stage, ... / The cycle starts when...
Next, ... / Following this, ... / After that, ... / At the next stage, ... / Once X has been done, ...
..., after which ... / ..., before being ... / After being V3, ... / At the same time, ...
Finally, ... / In the final stage, ... / The process ends when... / The cycle then begins again.

x: Then the leaves are rolled. Then they are fermented. Then they are dried.
The leaves are then rolled and left to ferment, after which they are dried with hot air.
Firstly, clay is dug. Secondly, it is sieved. Thirdly, it is mixed.
The process begins when clay is dug up. It is then sieved and mixed with sand and water.
After the sorting, then the tea is packed.
Once the tea has been sorted, it is packed.
Start with a noun phrase: 'After fermentation, ...', 'Following the drying stage, ...'
Use a time clause: 'Once the pulp is clean, ...', 'When the eggs hatch, ...'
Use a relative clause: '..., where it is heated to 1,000 C.'
Use a participle: 'After being cooled, ...', '..., before being delivered to shops.'

blocks.x: Three or four sequencers in a paragraph are enough. Not every sentence needs to start with a linker. A mid-sentence 'then', as in 'They are then...', sounds natural.
Do not use 'After that' and 'then' together in one sentence. 'After that, then it is packed' is wrong. Pick one.

blocks.q: Join into one sentence: The bricks are cooled. The bricks are packed.
blocks.a: 'Once the bricks have cooled, they are packed.' or 'After being cooled, the bricks are packed.'

pages.h: Writing the overview for a process

blocks.x: Because a process has no numbers, many students skip the overview. This is a serious mistake. Without an overview, it is hard to get above band 5 or 6 in Task Achievement. A process overview should say two things: how many stages there are or what kind of process it is, and the main idea from start to end.

x: Number of stages (if you are sure): 'There are eight main stages in the process.'
Start and end: 'from the picking of the leaves to the delivery of packed tea'
Type: linear or cycle, natural or man-made: 'This is a natural cycle that repeats itself.'
Main phases (optional): 'The first half involves preparing the raw material, while the second half focuses on packaging.'
Overall, the process is very interesting and has many steps.
Overall, the process consists of eight stages, beginning with the picking of fresh leaves and ending with the delivery of packed tea to shops.
In conclusion, frogs have a life cycle.
Overall, the frog passes through eight stages in a cycle lasting about 12 to 16 weeks, changing from a water-dwelling tadpole into a land-capable adult.
Overall, paper is recycled.
Overall, recycling paper is a nine-stage linear process in which waste paper is turned into pulp, cleaned and then formed into new sheets.

blocks.x: Put the overview straight after the introduction, as paragraph 2. This is where the examiner looks for it first. It can also go at the end, but placing it early means you know for certain it has been written.
Do not give an opinion in the overview. Statements such as 'This is an efficient process' or 'Recycling helps the environment' are not part of Task 1.

blocks.q: Write an overview for a 6-stage process showing how rainwater is collected from a roof, filtered, stored in a tank and pumped to a house.
blocks.a: Overall, the diagram shows a six-stage linear process in which rainwater is collected from a roof, cleaned and stored before being pumped into the house for domestic use.

blocks.x: Now look at a complete task. This diagram is linear and man-made, with 8 stages. Plan: introduction, overview, body 1 (stages 1 to 4: processing the leaves) and body 2 (stages 5 to 8: from drying to the shops).

The diagram below shows the stages in the production of black tea.

Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

Write at least 150 words.

c.title: The production of black tea
steps: Packed in boxes or tea bags

x: The diagram illustrates how black tea is produced, from the moment the leaves are picked to the point where the packed tea reaches shops.

Overall, the process consists of eight stages and is largely mechanical once the leaves have been harvested. Only the first step is carried out by hand, while the middle stages change the leaves physically and chemically before the tea is graded, packed and sent out.

The process begins when fresh tea leaves are picked by hand. They are then spread out and left to wither for 12 to 18 hours. Next, the withered leaves are rolled by machine and left to ferment, a stage known as oxidation. After fermentation, the leaves are dried with hot air, which completes the main processing stage.

Once the leaves are dry, they are sorted and graded according to their size. The graded tea is then packed, either loose in boxes or in tea bags, and in the final stage it is transported to shops, where it is sold to consumers.
notes: The introduction does not copy the prompt. 'Stages in the production' has become 'how black tea is produced'.
The overview gives the number of stages (eight) and the character of the process (largely mechanical, with only the first step done by hand).
The passive is used consistently: are picked, are rolled, is transported. There is no active 'workers pick'.
The sequencers vary: begins when, then, Next, After fermentation, Once the leaves are dry, in the final stage.
The two body paragraphs split at a logical point: preparation versus finishing.
Details from the diagram (12 to 18 hours, boxes or tea bags) are reported accurately.

blocks.x: If the diagram says '12-18 hours', write 'for 12 to 18 hours'. If you leave out the numbers, you lose marks for both accuracy and detail.

In a natural cycle the verbs are mostly active, because nature does the work by itself. This diagram has 8 stages, and the last stage leads back to the first. The overview must include the word 'cycle' and the total time.

The diagram below shows the life cycle of a frog.

Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

Write at least 150 words.

c.title: The life cycle of a frog

x: The diagram shows the life cycle of a frog, from the laying of eggs to the stage at which a fully grown frog is ready to reproduce.

Overall, there are eight main stages in this natural cycle, which takes roughly 12 to 16 weeks to complete. The most striking feature is the gradual change from a tadpole that lives in water and breathes through gills into an adult that can survive on land.

The cycle starts when an adult frog lays a mass of eggs, known as spawn, in water. After about ten days, tadpoles hatch from these eggs, and at this early point they breathe through gills. Their back legs then start to grow at around six to nine weeks, and by roughly the twelfth week the front legs have also appeared.

In the following stage, the tail shrinks and the young animal develops lungs, which allows it to breathe air. It is now a froglet and leaves the water. Finally, it grows into an adult frog at 12 to 16 weeks, and the cycle begins again when this frog lays its own eggs.
notes: Because this is a natural process, the verbs are active: hatch, grow, appear, shrinks, develops. The passive is not forced.
The overview mentions the cycle, the eight stages and the total time (12 to 16 weeks), plus the main change (from water to land).
The time details are accurate: about ten days, six to nine weeks, twelfth week.
'by roughly the twelfth week the front legs have also appeared' uses the present perfect to show grammatical range.
The last sentence closes the cycle ('the cycle begins again'), which a cycle diagram always needs.
Synonyms are used (young animal, froglet, adult frog) without changing the meaning.

blocks.x: In a life cycle, do not mix 'is born' and 'is hatched'. When something comes out of an egg, use the active verb 'hatch'. 'The frog is grown' is also wrong. Write 'The frog grows into an adult'.

blocks.q: Rewrite in better style: 'Then the tadpole gets back legs. Then it gets front legs.'
blocks.a: 'The tadpole then develops back legs, followed a few weeks later by front legs.'

title: Maps
bn: Comparing two maps: a complete formula for location, change and tense
goal: This chapter shows you how to compare two maps, use location and change vocabulary accurately, and write a clear overview for a map task.

blocks.x: In a map task you see two maps, or sometimes three. The job itself is simple: report what has changed and what has stayed the same, and say where each thing is. There are no numbers, so your vocabulary and your tenses decide your score.

head: Task type
What you see
Main tense
rows: Past simple or past perfect: 'was demolished', 'had been built by 2020'
A campus now and its planned layout
Future forms: 'will be extended', 'is to be converted'
Two possible sites for a new supermarket
Present simple + modals: 'Site A is close to...', 'it would be...'

x: First look at the title and the name of each map (the year or the plan). This tells you which tense to use.
Look for the north arrow. If there is none, treat the top of the map as north.
Put the two maps side by side and compare them item by item: what is new, what has gone, what has changed and what is the same.
Group the changes by area: north versus south, or east versus west of a road.

blocks.x: Make a quick list with four headings: NEW (built), GONE (demolished or removed), CHANGED (converted or extended) and SAME. Both your overview and your body paragraphs come out of these four lists.
If you treat a map like a year-by-year chart and write two separate descriptions ('In 1990... In 2020...'), the comparison is lost. For each area, describe the before and the after together.
If you cannot say where something is, the reader will not know which building you mean. Use compass directions and position phrases accurately. Practise the phrases below with the sample map.

c.title: Town centre (location practice)
