a short distance from / far from / on the edge of / on the outskirts of

x: The bank is near the library.
The bank is next to the library, on the north side of High Street.
The park is up and right.
The park is in the north-east of the town centre.
The lake is down of the road.
The lake lies to the south of High Street, between the school and the hospital.

blocks.x: 'In the north of the town' means inside the town, in its northern part. 'To the north of the town' means outside the town, in the northern direction. If you mix these up, your meaning will be wrong.

blocks.q: Using the sample map, describe where the hospital is.
blocks.a: The hospital is in the south-east of the town centre, south of High Street and to the east of the lake.

blocks.q: Using the sample map, describe where the library is in one sentence with two location phrases.
blocks.a: The library is in the north-west corner of the town centre, directly to the west of the bank.

blocks.x: Change is the core of a map task. If you repeat the same verb ('was built, was built, was built'), your Lexical Resource score drops. Learn the verbs in the table below in the passive form, because we usually do not know, or do not need to know, who made the change.

head: Change
Verb (passive)
Example
rows: was demolished / was knocked down / was pulled down
was converted into / was turned into / was made into
The post office was converted into a cafe.
One thing in place of another
was replaced by / made way for
The woodland was replaced by a car park.
was extended / was expanded / was enlarged
was reduced in size / was cut back
The park was reduced in size.
was built / was constructed / was opened / was added
was relocated to / was moved to
The bus station was relocated to the edge of town.
was cleared / was planted / was filled in
Trees were cleared and the pond was filled in.
was widened / was extended / was rerouted

x: The factory is not there now. There are apartments.
The factory has been demolished, and apartments have been built in its place.
The shops became bigger.
The row of shops has been extended southwards to form a shopping centre.
They cut the trees and made a car park.
The woodland has been cleared to make way for a car park.
The post office is now cafe.
The post office has been converted into a cafe.

blocks.x: Mix in some active verbs for variety: 'The town has expanded northwards', 'A footpath now runs along the river', 'The housing estate occupies the former farmland'.

Both 'was converted to a cafe' and 'converted into' are fine. For maps, 'was replaced by' sounds more natural than 'was replaced with'. Also, 'demolished' is only for buildings. For trees, use 'cut down' or 'cleared'.

blocks.q: Rewrite with a better verb: 'The trees were demolished and houses came.'
blocks.a: 'The trees were cut down, and houses were built on the land.' (or 'The trees were cleared to make way for housing.')

blocks.x: Tense errors are the most common band 6 problem in map tasks. Decide on the tense from the names of the maps, then keep it the same from start to finish.

head: Maps show
Tense
Example
rows: The farmland has been replaced by a housing estate.
Past simple passive (or past perfect with 'by')
The huts were demolished. By 2020, a hotel had been built.
Future passive: will be / is to be / is set to be / is planned to be
The pond will be filled in, and a cafe is to be built there.
remained / has remained / will remain unchanged
The main building will remain as it is.

x: The pond is filled and a cafe is built.
The pond will be filled in, and a cafe will be built in its place.
In 2020 the farmland becomes a golf course.
By 2020, part of the farmland had been turned into a golf course.
The road has been widened in 2010.
The road was widened in 2010. (specific past time, so past simple)

blocks.x: On a plan map, do not repeat 'will be' every time. Mix it with 'is to be extended', 'is set to be replaced', 'there are plans to build' and 'is going to be converted'.
Do not use the present perfect with a specific past year. 'Has been built in 2005' is wrong. When there is a year, use the past simple: 'was built in 2005'.

blocks.q: Maps: 'Now' and 'Proposed'. Correct: 'The car park has been replaced by student housing.'
blocks.a: 'The car park will be replaced by student housing.' (proposed change, so future)

pages.h: Overview and paragraph plan for maps

blocks.x: A map overview should give two or three big-picture ideas: how the area has changed overall (more urban, more residential, more focused on tourism), what has stayed the same, and where the biggest change is.

x: Introduction: say what the maps show, paraphrasing the place and the time (1 sentence).
Overview: the overall change in character plus what has stayed the same (2 sentences).
Body 1: all the changes in one area, for example north of the road.
Body 2: all the changes in another area (south of the road), plus any new roads or paths.
You do not need a conclusion. The overview already does that job.
Overall, there are many changes in the town.
Overall, the town has become far more residential and commercial, while the road network and the river have stayed the same.
Overall, some buildings are demolished and some are built.
Overall, the village was transformed from a farming community into a tourist resort, with most changes taking place along the coast.
Overall, the college will change a lot.
Overall, the college will gain several buildings at the expense of open space, although the main building and entrance will remain unchanged.

blocks.x: Divide the body paragraphs by area, not by type of change. The reader follows the map as they read, so moving from 'north of Main Road' to 'south of Main Road' is easy to follow.
Leave small details, such as a playground, out of the overview. The overview is for the big picture. Small details go in the body.

blocks.q: Map change list: farmland becomes housing, woodland becomes car park, factory becomes apartments, park smaller, roads unchanged. Write one overview sentence.
blocks.a: Overall, the town has become much more built up, with farmland, woodland and part of the park lost to development, although the road layout has not changed.

blocks.x: These maps show 1990 and 'today', so the main tense is the present perfect passive. Plan: introduction, overview, body 1 (north of Main Road) and body 2 (south of Main Road plus the river path).

The maps below show the town of Kingsbridge in 1990 and today.

Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

Write at least 150 words.

c.title: Kingsbridge town, 1990 and today

x: The maps compare the layout of the town of Kingsbridge in 1990 with its layout today.

Overall, the town has become far more residential and commercial, with most of the green space north of Main Road replaced by buildings. The road network and the river have stayed the same, and the houses in the south-east are also unchanged.

The biggest changes have taken place north of Main Road. The farmland in the north-west has been cleared to make way for a large housing estate, while the woodland in the north-east has been replaced by a car park. Between these two areas, the post office has been converted into a cafe, and the row of shops next to it has been extended southwards to form a shopping centre.

South of Main Road, the factory in the south-west has been demolished and apartments have been built in its place. The park has been reduced in size, as part of it is now a playground. Finally, a new footpath has been constructed along the northern bank of the river, and Bridge Lane, which runs south from Main Road, now connects to it.
notes: The tense is fully consistent: present perfect passive (has been cleared, has been replaced, has been demolished).
The change verbs vary: cleared to make way for, replaced by, converted into, extended, demolished, reduced in size, constructed.
The overview gives both the big trend (more residential and commercial) and the features that did not change.
Every change has a location phrase: in the north-west, between these two areas, next to it, along the northern bank.
The body is split by area (north and south of Main Road), so the reader can follow it easily.
No reasons or opinions that are not on the map have been added.

blocks.x: It is good to mention features that did not change, but saying so once in the overview is enough. In the body, write only about the changes.
Here one map shows the present and the other shows a plan, so you need future forms. Mix 'will be' with 'is to be' and 'is set to be' to avoid repetition.

The maps below show the present layout of Greenfield College and the changes that are planned for the site.

Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

Write at least 150 words.

c.title: Greenfield College: present site and planned changes

x: The maps show the current layout of Greenfield College and the changes that are planned for the site.

Overall, the college will have more buildings and less open space, as the garden, the pond and part of the sports field are set to be built over. The main building, the entrance path and Station Road will remain as they are.

In the northern half of the site, the library in the north-west will be extended eastwards, and the pond to its east is to be filled in to make room for a cafe. In the north-east, the western part of the sports field will be used for a new sports hall, leaving a much smaller playing field beside it.

In the southern half, the main change concerns how the land is used. The garden in the south-west is to be turned into a car park, while the existing car park in the south-east will be replaced by student housing. A group of trees will be planted between the entrance path and the new housing, and a cycle path will be laid along the south-western edge of the site, parallel to Station Road.
notes: The future forms vary: will be extended, is to be filled in, are set to be built over, is to be turned into.
The overview makes the main trend clear (more buildings, less open space) and says what will stay the same.
Change and location appear together: 'the pond to its east', 'the western part of the sports field', 'the south-western edge'.
The move of the car park is explained clearly in two steps: the garden becomes a car park, and the old car park becomes housing.
The body is split into the northern half and the southern half, which is the natural order for reading the map.
No item in the plan is missed: library, cafe, sports hall, field, car park, housing, trees, cycle path.

blocks.x: Do not write 'has been built' on a plan map, because nothing has happened yet. Every change is in the future, and for unchanged items you use 'will remain'.

blocks.q: Write one sentence about the sports field using 'make way for'.
blocks.a: Part of the sports field will make way for a new sports hall, so only a narrow playing field will remain.

title: Mistakes, checklist and band 7 strategy
bn: 33 common mistakes Bangladeshi students make, a final checklist and a 2-minute check
goal: In this chapter you will learn which Task 1 mistakes keep you at band 6, how to check your answer in 2 minutes, and how to control your word count.

blocks.x: To get band 7 in Task Achievement, you need a clear overview, a good selection of key features and accurate reporting of the numbers. The mistakes below cost the most marks in this criterion.

head: Mistake
Fix
rows: No overview, or one weak line at the end
Write a separate overview paragraph right after the introduction, with 2 main trends or features.
Copying the prompt word for word in the introduction
Paraphrase: change words and structure ('shows the number of' to 'illustrates how many').
Report only what the chart shows. No causes, no predictions unless the chart has them.
Wrong numbers or missing units (40 instead of 40 million)
Check every figure against the chart and always add the unit: %, million, tonnes, hours.
Select: highest, lowest, biggest change, exceptions, crossing points.
Link figures: 'twice as high as', 'whereas', 'compared with', 'the gap narrowed'.
Past data: past simple. Future projections: 'is expected to', 'will'. Processes: present simple.
Conclusion with an opinion ('This is a good sign')
No opinion in Task 1. Put the summary in the overview and skip a separate conclusion.
Ignoring one chart in a mixed task
Mention both charts in the introduction and overview, and give each a body paragraph.

x: The graph shows the number of tourists who visited three countries between 2000 and 2020.
The line graph illustrates how many international tourists travelled to three countries over a twenty-year period.
Car use fell because petrol became expensive.
Car use fell from 52% to 40% between 2005 and 2020.
In 2000 it was 20, in 2005 it was 26, in 2010 it was 34, in 2015 it was 40.
Gas output doubled from 20 to 40 TWh between 2000 and 2015.

blocks.q: What is wrong? 'Overall, the chart is very informative and shows many changes.'
blocks.a: It says nothing about the data. A real overview names the main trend, for example: 'Overall, gas remained the main source of electricity, while solar power grew the fastest.'

blocks.x: Coherence means the reader can follow you easily. Adding more linkers does not improve coherence. It makes your writing sound mechanical. The band 7 descriptor asks for a 'range of cohesive devices', but it still allows 'some under or over-use'. In other words, natural use is what counts.

head: Mistake
Fix
rows: Four paragraphs: introduction, overview, body 1, body 2.
A linker at the start of every sentence (Firstly, Secondly, In addition, Lastly)
Use fewer linkers and place some mid-sentence: 'Coal, by contrast, fell.'
Going year by year (In 2000... In 2005... In 2010...)
Group by trend or category: describe one line from start to end, then the next.
Repeating 'It can be seen that' or 'From the graph we can see that'
Start with the data subject: 'Bus use fell steadily.'
Bullet points or headings in the answer
Full sentences and paragraphs only. Bullets lose marks in Coherence.
Use it only when two lists match in order: 'A and B rose to 30% and 40% respectively.'

x: Firstly, car use rose. Secondly, bus use fell. Thirdly, cycling dropped. Lastly, metro use grew.
Car use rose until 2005, whereas bus use fell throughout. Cycling dropped at first, while the metro grew steadily.
From the graph we can see that coal fell. It can be seen that solar rose.
Coal production fell after 2012, while solar output rose sharply.
The figures for A and B were 30% and 40% respectively and C rose respectively.
The figures for A and B were 30% and 40% respectively, and C also rose.

blocks.x: Start each body paragraph with a topic phrase, such as 'Turning to the metro, ...' or 'The other two activities took up much less time.' The reader then knows at once what the paragraph is about.

blocks.q: Fix the cohesion: 'In 2010 sales were 50. In 2010 profits were 20. In 2015 sales were 70. In 2015 profits were 25.'
blocks.a: 'Sales rose from 50 to 70 between 2010 and 2015, while profits increased more modestly, from 20 to 25.'

blocks.x: These mistakes are very common in writing by Bangladeshi students, because many phrases are translated directly from Bangla. Once you can spot them, they are easy to fix.

head: Mistake
Fix
rows: Countable nouns take 'number of'. 'Amount of' is for uncountable things: water, money, electricity.
Say 'rose by 10 percentage points' (or 'rose from 20% to 30%'). A 10% increase on 20% is only 22%.
rise, rose, risen. 'Raise' needs an object: 'The government raised taxes.'
Match the size: slightly, gradually, steadily, considerably, sharply.
IELTS readers use international units: 1 lakh = 100,000; 1 crore = 10 million.

x: The amount of students increased dramatically from 820 to 840.
The number of students increased slightly, from 820 to 840.
Near about 3 crore people used the metro.
Nearly 30 million people used the metro.
The percentage rised 5% from 10% to 15%.
The percentage rose by five percentage points, from 10% to 15%.

blocks.x: Write 'doubled' only when the figure has actually become twice as large. A rise from 20 to 30 is not 'doubled'. It 'rose by half' or 'increased by 50%'.

blocks.q: Correct: 'The informations shows that more higher amount of peoples used bus in 2000 year.'
blocks.a: 'The data shows that a higher number of people used the bus in 2000.' ('The data show' is also correct.)

blocks.x: For band 7 in Grammatical Range and Accuracy, you need 'frequent error-free sentences'. This means most of your sentences should have no mistakes. The errors below are small, but if they keep appearing, they pull your score down.

head: Mistake
Fix
rows: 'The number of...' takes a singular verb: 'The number of students was...' ('A number of students were' is different.)
'reached to 50%', 'peaked at the highest point of 50%'
Wrong preposition after rise or fall
'rose to 50%' (end point), 'rose by 10%' (amount), 'a rise of 10%', 'a rise in sales'.
'The number of cars increased.' Also 'the highest', 'the bus', 'the metro'.
Write 'did not', 'was not' in academic writing.
Comma splice: 'Sales rose, they peaked in 2010.'
'Sales rose and peaked in 2010.' or 'Sales rose, peaking in 2010.'
Spelling: goverment, enviroment, recieve, untill, begining, fourty
government, environment, receive, until, beginning, forty.

x: The number of visitors were increased to 150 thousands in 2024.
The number of visitors increased to 150,000 in 2024.
Between 2016 to 2020 attendance fell, it reached to 40,000.
Between 2016 and 2020, attendance fell, reaching a low of 40,000.
Coal didn't changed much compare to gas.
Coal did not change much compared with gas.

blocks.x: When 'increase' is intransitive, it cannot be passive. 'The number was increased' (someone raised it) and 'The number increased' (it rose by itself) mean different things. For charts, the active 'increased' is usually correct.

blocks.q: Find the errors: 'In compare with 2010, the number of cars were rised by 2015.'
blocks.a: 'Compared with 2010, the number of cars had risen by 2015.' Errors: 'In compare with', 'were' (should be singular), 'rised' (risen), plus passive is wrong here.

blocks.x: The band descriptors are public. The table below is a simple version of the official descriptors and shows the main differences between band 6 and band 7. You are at 6 now, so aim for the right-hand column.

head: Criterion
Band 6 (roughly)
Band 7 (roughly)
rows: Overview present but data may be patchy; some details irrelevant or inaccurate
Clear overview of main trends or differences; key features clearly presented and highlighted
Arranged logically, but linkers can be mechanical or faulty
Logical organisation with clear progression; range of linkers with only some over-use
Adequate range; some errors in word choice or spelling
Enough range for flexibility; some less common items; awareness of collocation; occasional errors
Mix of simple and complex forms; some errors
Variety of complex structures; frequent error-free sentences; good control

x: Overview: 2 main features in every answer, in a separate paragraph.
Selection: 6 to 10 key numbers, each one with a comparison.
Language: 3 or 4 less common collocations (rose steadily, a marginal fall, overtook), used naturally rather than forced.
Grammar: at least 3 complex sentences (while, which, after -ing, reaching...), with the rest simple but clean.
Accuracy: catch grammar and number errors in your final 2-minute check.

blocks.x: You do not need rare words for band 7. A clean, accurate sentence such as 'Rose sharply to a peak of 52% in 2005' is far better than 'skyrocketed astronomically'.
Examiners recognise memorised templates ('The given graph delineates the information about...') straight away. A simple, accurate paraphrase earns more marks.
When you finish writing, keep 2 minutes for checking. This is not the time to add new ideas. It is only for finding mistakes. Learn this checklist by heart before the exam.

x: Introduction: the prompt is paraphrased, not copied, and it includes the chart type and the time period.
Overview: a separate paragraph with 2 main features and no specific numbers.
Body: every key feature has the correct number and unit.
Comparison: each body paragraph has at least 2 comparisons.
Tense: it matches the time on the chart (past, future, or present for a process).
No opinion, no reason, no conclusion with judgement.
Word count is between 170 and 200.
Paragraphs are clear: 4 blocks, separated by a blank line or an indent.
30 seconds: numbers. Check every number against the chart and make sure it has a unit.
30 seconds: verbs. Subject-verb agreement (the number was), tense, rose/risen.
30 seconds: small words. a/an/the, prepositions (to, by, of, in), plural -s.
30 seconds: spelling of words you used often (government, increase, approximately, proportion).

blocks.x: In computer-delivered IELTS the word count is often shown on screen, so you need to worry less about it. In the paper-based test you have to estimate it yourself. The method is on the next page.
While checking, do not try to rewrite whole sentences. Big changes bring in new mistakes. Make small fixes: one word, one ending.

blocks.q: You have 2 minutes left and you notice your overview is missing. What do you do?
blocks.a: Write a 2-sentence overview at the end of the introduction or as a short paragraph after it (use an arrow if on paper). A missing overview costs more than any small grammar error.

blocks.x: The minimum is 150 words. If you write fewer than 150, you are penalised in Task Achievement. On the other hand, writing 250 wastes time, leaves less time for Task 2 and increases your mistakes. Target: **170 to 200 words**.

head: Minutes
What to do
rows: Read the task, find 2 main features for the overview, choose 6 to 10 key numbers, plan paragraphs
Finish any missing comparison; make sure everything is in paragraphs
2-minute check: numbers, verbs, small words, spelling

x: Paper-based counting method: find out how many words fit on one line in your normal handwriting (usually 9 to 12). Lines x average = estimate.
Count exactly once while practising. Then in the exam you will have a feel for your 'line count'.
Count your first 3 practice answers in full and remember how many lines 170 words take.
Writing 260 words that repeat every number
Writing 185 words that select and compare key numbers
Stopping at 140 words to save time
Adding one comparison sentence to pass 150 safely

blocks.x: Do not spend more than 20 minutes on Task 1. Task 2 carries double weight, so protect your 40 minutes for it. If you take 25 minutes on Task 1, you risk losing marks in Task 2.
Examiners do not count words copied from the prompt. If you copy the prompt in your introduction, your 'real' word count drops and may fall below 150.

blocks.q: Your handwriting averages 10 words per line. Your answer has 4 paragraphs of 4, 3, 6 and 5 lines. Is it long enough?
blocks.a: 4 + 3 + 6 + 5 = 18 lines x 10 = about 180 words. Yes, it is safely above 150.

title: Practice bank
bn: 8 full practice tasks, each with a band 8 model answer and notes
goal: Here you will write 8 real-style Task 1 answers yourself, compare them with the models, and learn how to lift your own answer to band 7+.

pages.h: How to use this practice bank

blocks.x: This chapter has 8 tasks: 2 line graphs, 1 bar chart, 1 pie chart, 1 table, 1 mixed chart, 1 process and 1 map. Write each task yourself first, then look at the model. If you read the model first, you lose half the value of the practice.

x: Set a timer for 20 minutes. Put your phone away.
Read the task and plan for 3 minutes: 2 features for the overview, the key numbers and the paragraph split.
Write, do the 2-minute check and look at your word count.
Now read the model. Compare your overview with the model overview: did you pick out the same main features?
Read the notes, then rewrite 3 sentences from your answer in the style of the model.

blocks.x: One task a day is enough. Finish this bank in 8 days, then check all 8 of your answers again with the checklist from the previous chapter.

pages.h: Practice 1: line graph with four lines

blocks.x: When a chart has four lines, describing each line separately makes the answer long and dull. Group them instead: car and bus (falling after a peak, or falling), and bicycle and metro (rising towards the end).

The graph below shows the percentage of commuters in one city who used four different modes of transport to travel to work between 1990 and 2020.

Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

Write at least 150 words.

c.title: Percentage of commuters using four modes of transport in one city, 1990-2020

x: The line graph illustrates how commuters in one city travelled to work between 1990 and 2020, comparing the share who used cars, buses, bicycles and the metro.

Overall, the car remained the most common way to commute throughout the period, although its popularity peaked in 2005 and then declined. The metro showed the strongest growth, while bus use fell steadily and cycling recovered after an early drop.

In 1990, 42% of commuters drove to work, and this figure rose to a high of 52% in 2005. After that, it fell back gradually to 40% in 2020. The bus was the second most popular option at the start, used by 35% of workers, but its share decreased in every period, ending at just 21%.

The metro carried only 8% of commuters in 1990 and 1995, yet its share climbed to 22% by 2020, overtaking the bus in the final year. Cycling followed a different pattern: it dropped from 15% to a low of 9% in 2005, then rose again to 17%, although it was still the least common choice in 2020.
notes: The overview covers the main movement of all 4 lines together: car at the top, metro with the fastest growth, bus falling and cycling recovering.
It picks out the crossing point (the metro overtaking the bus in 2020), which is a key feature.
The peak and the low are given with exact years: 52% in 2005, 9% in 2005.
The verbs vary: rose, fell back, decreased, climbed, dropped, overtaking.
Body 1 covers the falling or peaking lines and body 2 covers the rising lines, so the grouping is logical.

pages.h: Practice 2: line graph with a new source

blocks.x: When a line starts at 0, you need phrases such as 'made no contribution', 'from nothing' or 'was not used at all'. Where two lines cross, mention it in the overview or the body.

The graph below shows the amount of electricity generated from gas, coal and solar power in one country between 2000 and 2024.

Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

Write at least 150 words.

c.title: Electricity generated from three sources in one country, 2000-2024

x: The line graph compares the amount of electricity a country produced from gas, coal and solar power between 2000 and 2024, measured in terawatt hours (TWh).

Overall, gas was by far the largest source of electricity throughout the period, and its output more than doubled. Solar power grew from nothing to become the second largest source, whereas coal declined after 2012.

Gas-fired generation stood at 20 TWh in 2000 and increased steadily, reaching a peak of 50 TWh in 2020 before dipping slightly to 48 TWh in 2024. Coal, by contrast, produced 12 TWh at the start and rose only modestly to 15 TWh in 2008, where it stayed until 2012. From then on, it fell in each period, ending at 8 TWh.

Solar power made no contribution in 2000 and 2004, and its output remained very small, at 1 to 2 TWh, until 2012. After this point, however, it rose sharply, to 12 TWh in 2020 and 18 TWh in 2024. As a result, solar had overtaken coal by 2020 and generated more than twice as much electricity as coal by the end of the period.
notes: The unit (TWh) is written in full once in the introduction and in short form after that.
Both 'more than doubled' and 'more than twice as much' are mathematically correct (20 to 48, 18 vs 8).
'had overtaken coal by 2020' uses the past perfect, which shows grammatical range.
The stable phase ('where it stayed until 2012') is not missed.
Contrast linkers appear in natural places: by contrast, however, whereas.

pages.h: Practice 3: bar chart by age group

blocks.x: In this bar chart the categories (age groups) are on the x-axis. The main story is that two activities move in opposite directions. If you capture this in the overview, half the work is done.

The chart below shows the average number of hours per week that people in four age groups spent on four leisure activities.

Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

Write at least 150 words.

c.title: Average hours per week spent on four leisure activities, by age group

x: The bar chart shows the average number of hours people in four age groups spent each week on social media, television, sport and reading.

Overall, younger people devoted most of their free time to social media, while older people spent the most time watching TV. Time spent on sport fell with age, whereas reading became more popular in older groups.

The 15-24 age group spent 18 hours a week on social media, the highest figure in the chart. This dropped sharply with age, to 11 hours among 25 to 44-year-olds, 6 hours for those aged 45-64 and just 3 hours for people over 65. Television showed the reverse pattern, rising from 7 hours for the youngest group to 20 hours for the oldest, which made it the top activity for both of the older groups.

The other two activities took up much less time. Young people played sport for 6 hours a week, but this halved to 3 hours in the 45-64 group and fell to only 2 hours among the over-65s. Reading moved in the opposite direction, increasing from 3 hours to 8 hours across the four age groups.
notes: The overview gives the direction of all 4 activities: social media down, TV up, sport down, reading up.
The biggest figure (18 hours) and the biggest value overall (20 hours) are both clearly highlighted.
The language for age groups varies: the 15-24 age group, 25 to 44-year-olds, those aged 45-64, the over-65s.
'halved' is accurate (6 to 3), and 'reverse pattern' and 'opposite direction' create comparisons.
The body is split into the large activities (social media, TV) and the small ones (sport, reading).

blocks.x: Two pie charts show the shares at two points in time. If the biggest slice changes (from food to housing), that is the main feature. When you describe a change in percentages, use 'percentage points' correctly.

The pie charts below show how the average household in one country spent its money in 2000 and 2020.

Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

Write at least 150 words.

c.title: Average household spending in one country, 2000 and 2020

x: The pie charts compare how the average household in one country divided its spending between six categories in 2000 and 2020.

Overall, food was the biggest expense in 2000, but by 2020 housing had taken its place. The shares spent on housing, transport, education and health all grew, while food and other items took up a smaller part of the budget.

In 2000, food accounted for 38% of household spending, considerably more than housing, which made up 22%. Twenty years later, the proportion spent on food had fallen to 26%, while housing costs had risen to 30%, making housing the largest single category. The gap between these two categories therefore reversed, from 16 points in favour of food to 4 points in favour of housing.

The remaining categories were much smaller. Transport rose from 12% to 15% of spending, and the share devoted to education went up from 8% to 11%. Health showed a similar increase of three percentage points, from 6% to 9%. In contrast, the 'other' category dropped from 14% to 9%, so in 2020 it was equal to health and slightly below education.
notes: The main feature (food and housing swapping places) appears in both the overview and body 1.
'percentage points' is used correctly: 6% to 9% is three percentage points.
The language for shares varies: accounted for, made up, the proportion spent on, the share devoted to.
The small categories are grouped together in one paragraph, so the answer does not become too long.
The comparison for 2020 (other equal to health, below education) shows that the writer is analysing the data.

blocks.x: A table has many numbers, so it tests your selection skills. Give the start and end of each row, and point out any row that moves in a different direction. You do not need every number in between.

The table below shows the number of students enrolled in four courses at one university in 2010, 2015 and 2020.

Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

Write at least 150 words.

c.title: Number of students enrolled in four courses at one university

x: The table gives the number of students enrolled in four university courses in 2010, 2015 and 2020.

Overall, Computer Science grew the fastest and became the most popular course, while English Literature was the only subject to lose students steadily. Business and Engineering changed relatively little.

Computer Science had 820 students in 2010, but this figure rose to 1,340 in 2015 and to 2,150 in 2020, more than two and a half times the original number. As a result, it overtook Business, which had been the largest course at the start with 1,500 students. Business enrolment rose slightly to 1,620 in 2015 before dipping to 1,580 in 2020, which left it 570 students behind Computer Science.

Engineering attracted 960 students in 2010 and saw modest growth, to 1,010 and then 1,180. English Literature, on the other hand, declined sharply. Its enrolment fell from 640 to 470 and then to 310, so by 2020 it had less than half the number of students it had a decade earlier.
notes: The overview names the three patterns in the table: the fastest growth, the only decline and the stable courses.
Math accurate: 2,150 is more than 2.5 times 820; 310 is less than half of 640.
The change in ranking ('overtook Business') is a key feature, and the answer picks it out.
The number format is correct: 1,340 and 2,150 (with commas), and no lakh or crore.
The past perfect in 'which had been the largest course' creates a complex sentence.

blocks.x: In a mixed task the two charts may or may not be related. Mention both in the introduction and the overview. This kind of task takes longer, so 3 or 4 key points from each chart are enough.

The line graph below shows the number of adults and children who visited the City Science Museum between 2016 and 2024. The pie chart shows the main reasons visitors gave for their visit in 2024.

Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

Write at least 150 words.

charts.title: Visitors to the City Science Museum, 2016-2024

x: The line graph shows the number of adults and children who visited the City Science Museum between 2016 and 2024, and the pie chart shows visitors' main reasons for coming in 2024.

Overall, visitor numbers for both groups rose apart from a sharp fall in 2020, and both had reached their highest levels by 2024. In that year, school trips and family days out were the most common reasons for a visit.

In 2016, the museum received 120,000 adult visitors and 80,000 children. These figures grew to 135,000 and 95,000 respectively in 2018. In 2020, however, attendance collapsed to only 40,000 adults and 25,000 children. Numbers then rebounded strongly, reaching 110,000 and 90,000 in 2022 and rising further to 150,000 adults and 130,000 children in 2024. The gap between the two groups narrowed over the period, from 40,000 to 20,000.

According to the 2024 survey, 34% of visitors came as part of a school trip and 28% for a family day out. Special exhibitions attracted 22%, while tourism accounted for 10% and other reasons for just 6%.
notes: The introduction mentions both charts, and the overview gives the main point of each.
The unit 'thousands' is converted into full numbers (120,000), which is clearer for the reader.
'respectively' is used correctly: the two lists are in the same order.
The narrowing gap (40,000 to 20,000) is a smart comparison. It is not written on the chart, but it can be calculated from it.
The pie paragraph is short, but it covers every slice accurately.

blocks.x: This is a linear process with 9 stages. The split point is between cleaning the pulp (stages 1 to 5) and making the sheets (stages 6 to 9). Use the present simple passive from start to finish.

The diagram below shows how recycled paper is made.

Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

Write at least 150 words.

c.title: How recycled paper is made
steps: Mixed with water to form pulp
Pressed between rollers to remove water
Cut into sheets and delivered to shops

x: The diagram illustrates the stages involved in turning used paper into new paper products that can be sold in shops.

Overall, there are nine stages in this linear process, beginning with the collection of waste paper and ending with the delivery of new paper to shops. The first half focuses on turning old paper into clean pulp, while the second half reforms this pulp into sheets.

First, used paper is collected and then sorted according to type and grade. It is then mixed with water to produce pulp. At the next stage, the ink is removed from the pulp in a process called de-inking, after which the pulp is cleaned further and whitened. By this point, the old paper has been fully converted into clean, white pulp.

Once the pulp is clean, it is pressed between rollers in order to remove the water. The pressed material then passes over heated rollers, which dry it. The dry paper is wound into large reels, and these are later cut into sheets. In the final step, the finished paper is delivered to shops.
notes: The overview gives the number of stages, the linear type, the start and the end, plus the two phases.
Passive range: is collected, is removed, are later cut, is delivered.
Sequencing vary: First, then, At the next stage, after which, Once, In the final step.
The technical term (de-inking) is taken from the diagram and explained, and no new information is added.
One active sentence ('passes over heated rollers') adds variety without changing the meaning.

blocks.x: Both 1980 and 2020 are in the past, so use the past simple passive. The main story is the change from a farming and fishing village to a tourist resort. Split the body into north of the road (inland) and south of the road (the coast).

The maps below show a coastal village in 1980 and 2020.

Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

Write at least 150 words.

c.title: A coastal village in 1980 and 2020

x: The maps show how a small coastal village changed between 1980 and 2020.

Overall, the village was transformed from a farming and fishing community into a tourist resort. Most of the farmland, the fishing huts and part of the forest gave way to tourist facilities, although the coast road and the main residential area remained.

In 1980, a large area of farmland covered the north-west of the village. By 2020, the western half of this land had become a golf course, while holiday apartments had been built on the eastern half. The village houses to the east of this area were extended southwards, and the forest in the north-east was reduced in size, with a car park built on the cleared land.

Along the coast, south of the coast road, the fishing huts were demolished and replaced by a larger hotel, and a new restaurant was built to the east of it. The jetty that ran out towards the sea was also removed, and a marina was constructed in roughly the same position.
notes: The overview gives both the change in character (from farming and fishing to tourism) and what stayed the same.
The past simple and the past perfect ('By 2020 ... had become') are mixed correctly.
The change verbs vary: gave way to, had been built, were extended, was reduced in size, were demolished, was constructed.
Every item has a location phrase: in the north-west, to the east of this area, south of the coast road.
The body is split into inland and coast, following the geography of the map.

blocks.x: When you finish the practice bank, write the overviews from all 8 of your answers on one page. If your overviews are strong, you are already well on the way to band 7.

title: Understanding the question
bn: Understand the prompt properly and half the work is done
goal: In this chapter you will learn how to recognise the five types of Task 2 question, separate the topic from the task, answer every part of the prompt and write a clear thesis.

blocks.x: In Task 2 you write an argumentative essay of at least 250 words in 40 minutes. It carries twice the weight of Task 1, so most of your Writing band comes from this task.

head: Fact
Detail
rows: 40 minutes recommended (20 for Task 1, 60 in total)
At least 250 words. Below 250 you lose marks in Task Response
The Task 2 score counts double the Task 1 score
Task Response, Coherence and Cohesion, Lexical Resource, Grammatical Range and Accuracy, each worth the same (25%)
Formal and academic, an argument that includes your own opinion; full paragraphs, no bullet points

blocks.x: This chapter deals only with the first criterion: **Task Response**. The examiner checks whether you have answered every part of the question, whether your position is clear and whether your ideas are developed.

Many students look at the prompt for ten seconds, spot the topic and start writing. Knowing the topic is 'technology' is not enough. If you do not understand what the question asks you to do (agree? discuss? solve?), you will stay at band 5 or 6, however good your English is.
Spend the first two or three minutes only reading the prompt. Underline the key words and write the question type in the margin. Those three minutes will save you ten later.

pages.h: The five question types at a glance

blocks.x: IELTS Task 2 prompts nearly always fall into one of five families. You can tell the type from the instruction line, which is the last line of the prompt.

head: Type
Typical instruction
What you must do
rows: To what extent do you agree or disagree? / Do you agree or disagree?
Take one clear position and keep it for the whole essay
Discuss both views and give your own opinion.
Explain both views, then give your own opinion
What are the advantages and disadvantages? / Do the advantages outweigh the disadvantages?
Explain both sides; if the prompt says 'outweigh', state which side is heavier
What are the causes? What solutions can you suggest? / What problems does this cause?
Cover exactly the two parts it asks for (cause + solution, problem + solution, cause + effect)
Why is this happening? Is this a positive or negative development?
Give a separate, direct answer to each question

blocks.x: The verbs in the last line are your boss: 'discuss', 'agree', 'outweigh', 'suggest', 'why'. If you misread these words, you get the type wrong.

blocks.q: Name the type: 'Some people say that zoos are cruel and should be closed. Others think they protect endangered animals. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.'
blocks.a: Discussion. You must explain both views (cruel vs protect) and then give your own opinion.

blocks.q: Name the type: 'Fewer young people are choosing to study science at university. What are the reasons for this? What can be done to encourage more students to choose science?'
blocks.a: Cause/solution (part of the problem/solution family). You need both parts: the reasons and the measures.

blocks.x: You are given a statement and must say how far you agree with it. You can agree completely, disagree completely or partly agree. Whichever you choose, it must stay the same from the introduction to the conclusion.
Some people believe that university education should be free for all students. To what extent do you agree or disagree?

x: 'Governments should spend more money on public transport than on building new roads. To what extent do you agree or disagree?'
'Children should be taught how to manage money at school. Do you agree or disagree?'
'The best way to improve public health is to increase the number of sports facilities. To what extent do you agree or disagree?'
'Social media companies should be held responsible for false information posted on their platforms. To what extent do you agree or disagree?'
'Unpaid community service should be a compulsory part of high school programmes. To what extent do you agree or disagree?'
'Some people think that a person's success depends mainly on hard work rather than luck. Do you agree or disagree?'

head: Your position
How the essay looks
rows: Two body paragraphs, each giving a different reason in support
Two body paragraphs, each giving a different reason against
Body 1: where you agree; Body 2: where you disagree; state the balance in the introduction

blocks.x: 'To what extent' means 'how far'. If you write 'I agree' and then give both sides equal weight in the body, the examiner will say your position is unclear. If you partly agree, say so in the introduction: 'I agree with this only in the case of ...'.
Some prompts look different but are still opinion questions, for example 'Is this a positive or negative development?' or 'Is this a good idea?'. These ask for a clear judgement too.
In an opinion essay, 'I believe' or 'In my view' once in the introduction and once in the conclusion is enough. You do not need 'I think' in every line.

pages.h: Type 2 and 3: Discussion, advantages and disadvantages

blocks.x: A **discussion** essay presents two views held by two groups. You must explain both views fairly. If the prompt says 'give your own opinion', you must then say which side you take. Without an opinion, Task Response drops to band 5 or 6.

x: 'Some people think that parents should teach children how to be good members of society. Others believe that school is the best place to learn this. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.'
'Some argue that the government should pay for the arts, while others think the money is better spent on health and education. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.'
'Some believe that older people should retire early to make room for the young, while others think they should keep working. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.'
'Some people prefer to live in a big city, while others prefer a small town. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.'

blocks.x: An **advantages/disadvantages** prompt describes a trend or change. It comes in two forms: 'What are the advantages and disadvantages?' on its own (an opinion is optional) and 'Do the advantages outweigh the disadvantages?' (a judgement is required).

x: 'More and more people are working from home. Do the advantages of this development outweigh the disadvantages?'
'Many students now study online instead of attending classes. What are the advantages and disadvantages of this?'
'Some companies are replacing human workers with robots. Do the benefits of this outweigh the drawbacks?'
'International tourism has grown rapidly in recent decades. Does this bring more benefits or more problems to local people?'

blocks.x: With an 'outweigh' question, many students list advantages and disadvantages but never say which side is heavier. Say it clearly in the introduction and the conclusion: 'I believe the drawbacks are more significant'.

blocks.q: 'Some people think tourists should pay more than local residents to visit museums. Others disagree. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.' How many body paragraphs do you need, and what goes in each?
blocks.a: Body 1: why tourists should pay more (local taxpayers already fund museums, tourist revenue). Body 2: why the price should be the same (fairness, culture should be open to all). Then give your own opinion in the introduction and conclusion, and at the end of Body 2 if you wish.

blocks.x: These types do not contain the word 'agree', so students often try to give an opinion and miss the real parts of the question. Give exactly the two things the prompt asks for.

head: Instruction pair
Body 1
Body 2
rows: What are the causes? What are the solutions?
Solutions (even better if they match the causes)
What problems does this cause? How can they be solved?
What are the causes? What are the effects?
Why is this happening? Is it positive or negative?
What are the reasons? What can individuals do?

x: 'In many cities, the amount of waste people produce is increasing. Why is this happening? What can be done to reduce it?'
'Obesity among children is rising in many countries. What are the causes of this, and what solutions can you suggest?'
'Many young people leave rural areas to work in cities. What problems does this cause? What can be done about it?'
'Many people today prefer to buy imported food rather than local produce. Why is this the case? Is this a positive or negative development?'
'People are reading fewer books than in the past. Why is this? What effects might this have on society?'
'Many students choose to study abroad. What are the benefits for the student? Are there any disadvantages for their home country?'

blocks.x: The question asks 'What can individuals do?' and you write 'The government should ...'. This is partly off-task. Take the answer to 'who should act' from the prompt itself.

In a two-part question, give one body paragraph to each question, and give a short answer to both questions in the introduction. After the first paragraph the examiner already knows you will answer both.

The **topic** is what the essay is about (for example, fast food). The **task** is what you must do with that topic (for example, explain the health problems caused by fast food and suggest solutions). For band 7 you need an essay on the exact task, not a general essay on the topic.

head: Prompt
Topic (broad)
Narrow focus
Task
rows: 'Advertising aimed at children should be banned. Agree or disagree?'
'Why do people in cities feel lonely? What can be done?'
'Some say history is a waste of time at school. Discuss both views.'
'More people are using cars. Do advantages outweigh disadvantages?'

x: Read the last instruction line first and identify the type.
Circle the topic word in the main statement (for example 'advertising').
Underline the limiting words: 'aimed at children', 'in cities', 'at school', 'in developing countries'.
Ask yourself: for whom, where, when? Do not go outside these limits.
Write the question in your own words in one line, then start planning.
Prompt: 'advertising aimed at children'. Essay: advertising in general is manipulative and wastes consumers' money.
Essay: advertisements designed for young children exploit their inability to recognise persuasive intent.
Prompt: 'loneliness in cities'. Essay: city life has many problems such as pollution, traffic and crime.
Essay: in large cities people often live alone in flats and rarely speak to their neighbours, which leaves many feeling isolated.
Prompt: 'history at school'. Essay: history is interesting and people visit museums to learn about it.
Essay: studying history at school teaches students to evaluate sources, a skill they need well beyond the classroom.

blocks.x: If you drop in a memorised essay, the topic may match but the task will not. Examiners spot this easily, and they can remove memorised language from your word count.

pages.h: Answering every part and writing the thesis

blocks.x: A prompt usually has two or three parts. If you miss one, Task Response cannot go above band 6, because the descriptor says 'addresses all parts of the task'.

head: Prompt wording
Hidden parts
rows: 'Discuss both views and give your own opinion'
View A, view B, your opinion = 3 parts
'What are the causes and what can be done?'
One part, but your position must be clear and consistent
'What are the advantages for individuals and for society?'

blocks.x: The **thesis** is the last sentence of the introduction, where you state the main answer of your essay. It should be a specific claim, not a vague promise.

x: It matches the question type (a position for an opinion question, a hint of the main cause and solution for a problem/solution question).
It previews the main idea of each body paragraph.
It paraphrases the prompt instead of copying its words.
It is no longer than one or two sentences.
This essay will discuss both sides of this issue.
While some argue that zoos are outdated, I believe well-run zoos are still justified because they protect species that would otherwise disappear.
There are many advantages and disadvantages of working from home.
In my view, the time and money saved by working from home outweigh the risk of isolation, provided employees still meet colleagues regularly.
I will explain the causes and solutions of obesity.
Children's weight gain is driven mainly by cheap processed food and inactive lifestyles, and both could be addressed through school-based action.
I partly agree and partly disagree.
I agree that basic financial skills belong in schools, but I do not think they should replace traditional subjects such as mathematics.

blocks.q: Fix this thesis: 'Nowadays technology is very important and has both good and bad sides.' Prompt: 'Do the advantages of online shopping outweigh the disadvantages?'
blocks.a: 'Although online shopping can encourage overspending, I believe its convenience and lower prices make it a clear benefit for most consumers.' (Topic narrowed to online shopping, position on 'outweigh' clear.)

blocks.x: Below is a simplified version of the public band descriptors. Remember that the key phrases for band 7 are 'clear position throughout' and 'extends and supports main ideas'.

head: Band
What the examiner sees
rows: Only some parts of the task are answered, the position is unclear or changes, and ideas are limited and repeated
All parts are answered but some are underdeveloped; there is a position but it is unclear in places; the conclusion is vague or repetitive
All parts are answered, the position is clear throughout, and main ideas are extended and supported, though some may be over-generalised
All parts are fully answered in a well-developed response, with relevant and well-supported ideas
A fully developed position, with fully extended and well-supported ideas

blocks.x: Most of the time, the gap between band 6 and band 7 is **development**. When you state an idea, explain why it is true and what follows from it, give a concrete example and link it back to the question. Without these, the idea stays a mere item in a list.

x: Online learning is flexible. It is also cheaper. Many people like it.

Online learning is flexible because recorded lectures allow students to study around part-time jobs. A student in Dhaka who works evenings, for example, can watch a lecture at midnight rather than missing it entirely.
Pollution is a big problem and it causes many diseases.
Air pollution from brick kilns and diesel vehicles is linked to asthma and other lung diseases, which places a heavy burden on public hospitals.

blocks.x: Over-generalisation: 'Everyone uses smartphones', 'All teenagers are addicted to games'. Claims like these are a band 7 weakness. Use 'most', 'many' or 'a large number of' instead.
Put no more than two main ideas in each body paragraph, each with an example. Two ideas explained in depth are better than four ideas touched on lightly.
Some people believe that university students should pay the full cost of their studies because a degree mainly benefits the individual. To what extent do you agree or disagree?

x: Who should pay for higher education is a politically sensitive question, and some argue that students themselves ought to cover the entire cost of their degrees, since they are the ones who later earn higher salaries. I largely disagree with this view: although graduates do gain personally, society gains at least as much, so the cost should be shared.

It is true that a degree often brings private rewards. Graduates in most economies earn considerably more over their working lives than people who left education at eighteen, and they tend to have more secure jobs. From this perspective, asking taxpayers who never attended university to fund someone else's advantage seems unfair. A student who goes on to become a corporate lawyer, for instance, could reasonably be expected to repay at least part of what her training cost.

However, this argument ignores the wider returns that education brings. A country needs doctors, engineers and teachers, and if training for these professions became extremely expensive, many talented young people from low-income families would simply not apply. The result would be a smaller and less diverse pool of professionals, which would harm everyone who relies on public services. Educated citizens also pay more tax and are more likely to take part in civic life, so the state recovers much of its investment indirectly.

A fairer approach would be a shared model in which the government pays a large portion of tuition and graduates contribute through an income-linked loan once they earn above a certain threshold. This would protect access for poorer students while still recognising the personal benefit of a degree.

In conclusion, although graduates clearly benefit as individuals, I do not believe they should bear the full cost of their studies, because the gains from higher education are spread across the whole of society.
notes: The position is clear in the introduction: 'I largely disagree', with the reason given in one line.
Body 1 accepts the opposite side fairly ('It is true that ...'), and Body 2 then gives a strong counter-argument. The position never changes.
Each idea is developed: claim, reason, result and an example (the corporate lawyer).
Body 3 offers a practical alternative, which gives a careful answer to 'to what extent'.
There is no over-generalisation: 'most economies', 'many talented young people'.
The conclusion adds no new ideas. It only restates the position and the main reason.

blocks.q: Find the thesis sentence of this essay and explain why it is 'largely disagree' and not 'partly agree'.
blocks.a: Thesis: 'I largely disagree with this view: although graduates do gain personally, society gains at least as much, so the cost should be shared.' The writer accepts the personal benefit but rejects the idea that students should pay the full cost, so the position is mostly disagreement.

title: Planning and structure
bn: Plan for 5 minutes, write for 35: no more confusion about structure
goal: This chapter shows you a paragraph plan for each question type, quick ways to find ideas, and how to write the introduction, body paragraphs and conclusion.

blocks.x: If you start writing without a plan, you run out of ideas halfway through and your body paragraphs start to repeat. Plan for five minutes and you can write calmly for the remaining 35.

head: Minutes
Job
rows: Read the prompt, identify the type, underline the key words
Brainstorm, choose your ideas, write a paragraph plan (in note form)
Check verb tenses, articles, plural s, spelling and whether your position is consistent

blocks.x: Writing 400 words does not earn extra marks. Longer essays contain more grammar mistakes and leave no time for checking. 270-310 words is the sweet spot.
Before the exam, count how many words ten lines of your handwriting hold. Then in the exam you will not need to count every word. You can tell from the number of lines whether you have passed 250.

These plans are not fixed rules, but they are safe and clear to the examiner. Four paragraphs (introduction, two body paragraphs, conclusion) are nearly always enough. Write five only when you have three strong ideas and enough time.

The five-paragraph option: three reasons in an opinion essay, or in a discussion essay View A, View B and a separate paragraph for your own opinion. With five paragraphs each body paragraph gets shorter, so there is a risk of weaker development.

In a discussion essay, if your opinion first appears in the conclusion, the examiner will say your position is 'only in conclusion'. State it once in the introduction, support it in Body 2 and confirm it in the conclusion.

blocks.q: Write a plan: 'Some people think that the government should invest more in space exploration. Others believe this money should be spent on problems on Earth. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.' (You support the Earth side.)
blocks.a: Intro: paraphrase both views + 'I believe urgent problems on Earth should come first'. Body 1: the benefits of space research (technology spin-offs such as satellite weather forecasting). Body 2: problems on Earth (poverty, climate adaptation), the opportunity cost, and my support. Conclusion: Earth first, though a limited space budget is acceptable.

blocks.x: For many students the problem is ideas, not English. If your mind goes blank in the exam hall, use the tools below. Do not spend more than three minutes brainstorming on any prompt.
