How it works
Quick example (topic: working from home)
rows: Employee saves time; company saves office rent; city has less traffic
Money, health, education, environment, society, culture, safety
Money: no transport cost; health: less stress or more loneliness
What happens now, and what happens in ten years
Now: comfort; later: weaker team culture
After each point, ask 'why?' or 'so what?' twice
Less commuting, so what? More sleep, better focus, fewer sick days
When you find an idea, think of its opposite

blocks.x: Some people believe that children should not be given smartphones until they are teenagers. To what extent do you agree or disagree?

x: Who: child, parents, school, society. Areas: health, education, safety, social life.

Raw list (one minute, no judging): eye strain, less sleep, addiction to games, cyberbullying, contact parents in emergency, educational apps, social pressure if friends have phones, less outdoor play.
Group them: AGAINST early phones = health/sleep, addiction, cyberbullying. FOR = safety contact, learning apps.
Decide your position: mostly agree (no smartphone before 13, a basic phone is fine).
Choose the two strongest ideas: Body 1 = damage to sleep and attention; Body 2 = the safety need can be met with a basic phone.
Think of one example for each: a child playing games past midnight before exams; a simple button phone that only calls parents.

blocks.x: You do not need real research to make an example. Realistic examples such as 'A child who ...', 'In my country, ...' or 'For instance, many families in Dhaka ...' are enough. Do not invent statistics ("78% of children").
If you brainstorm eight ideas, do not try to use all eight. Take the best two and go deeper. Drop the rest.

The introduction has two jobs: to restate the question in your own words (paraphrase) and to give your answer (position or thesis). You do not need background stories, quotations or 'In this modern era'.

x: Sentence 1: paraphrase the statement in the prompt (synonyms, changes in word form, changes in structure).
Sentence 2 (optional): in a discussion essay give the other view, or add a short piece of context.
Sentence 3: the thesis, your clear answer to this type of question.

head: Prompt words
Paraphrase options
rows: an increasing number of people / a growing proportion of the population
young people / those under the age of twelve / the younger generation
ought to be prohibited / should not be allowed
is on the rise / has grown considerably
remote working / doing one's job from home

x: Nowadays, technology is everywhere. Many people think children should not have smartphones until they are teenagers. I will discuss this in my essay.

It is often argued that children should not own a smartphone until they reach their teens. I largely agree, since early access tends to harm sleep and concentration, and a child's need to contact parents can be met in simpler ways.
In this modern era, working from home is a hot topic. There are advantages and disadvantages.
Remote working has become far more common since 2020. In my view, the benefits it brings to employees outweigh the drawbacks, as long as companies make an effort to keep teams connected.
Obesity is a very big problem nowadays. This essay will talk about causes and solutions.
Childhood obesity is rising in many countries. This essay argues that it stems mainly from processed food and inactive lifestyles, and that schools are well placed to tackle both.

blocks.x: The examiner does not include words copied from the prompt in your word count. If you copy 'Some people believe that children should not be given smartphones' word for word, those words do not count.

blocks.q: Write a paraphrase + position: 'Some people think that zoos should be closed because keeping animals in cages is cruel. To what extent do you agree or disagree?' (You disagree.)
blocks.a: 'Some argue that zoos are cruel and ought to be shut down. I disagree, because modern zoos play an important part in protecting endangered species, provided they meet strict welfare standards.'

pages.h: Body paragraphs: topic, explain, example, link

blocks.x: Each body paragraph is a mini essay. The safest structure is **topic sentence, explanation, example, link** (TEEL).

head: Part
Job
Sentences
rows: The main idea of the paragraph, directly connected to the question
Why or how; answers 'why?' and 'so what?'
Connects the idea back to your position or the question

head: Part
Sentence from a band 8 paragraph
rows: The strongest reason to delay smartphone ownership is its effect on sleep and concentration.
Games and social media apps are designed to keep users scrolling, and children are far less able than adults to stop on their own.
When a phone stays in the bedroom, the result is often lost sleep, which in turn makes it harder to pay attention in class the next day.
A ten-year-old who plays an online game until midnight before an exam, for example, is unlikely to perform at his best in the morning.
For this reason, I believe parents are right to keep these devices away from younger children.

x: The topic sentence connects directly to the prompt: 'delay smartphone ownership'.
The explanation is a chain of cause and effect: apps keep you scrolling, children cannot stop, sleep is lost, attention suffers.
The example is specific and realistic, with no invented statistics.
The link sentence confirms the position again, so the paragraph has a clear purpose.
Firstly, smartphones are bad. They are not good for children. Children use them a lot.
The strongest reason to delay smartphone ownership is its effect on sleep and concentration.
For example, 90% of children are addicted to phones.
A ten-year-old who plays an online game until midnight before an exam, for example, is unlikely to perform well.
So, this is why smartphones are bad.
For this reason, I believe parents are right to keep these devices away from younger children.

blocks.x: If you open with an example in place of a topic sentence ('For example, my cousin ...'), the main point of the paragraph gets lost. Make the claim first, then give the example.
The conclusion has two jobs: to restate your position and to remind the reader of your main reasons in one line. Never add a new idea or a new example, and never suddenly change your position.

x: In conclusion, there are many advantages and disadvantages, and people should think carefully about this topic.
In conclusion, although remote working can leave some employees feeling isolated, the time and money it saves make it a positive change overall.
To conclude, smartphones are bad, but they are also good, so it depends.
To sum up, I believe children are better off without a smartphone until their teens, because early use damages sleep and their safety can be ensured with a basic phone.
In conclusion, governments should also make strict laws against pollution and people should plant trees and use bicycles.
In conclusion, the rise in urban waste is driven mainly by single-use packaging, and a deposit scheme for bottles would be the most practical response.
In an opinion, discussion or outweigh essay, the conclusion must state your position.
In a problem/solution essay, give the main cause and the best solution in one line.
Two sentences are enough; 30-45 words.
Use one of 'In conclusion', 'To sum up' or 'Overall', and put a comma after 'In conclusion'.

blocks.x: Do not hand in an essay without a conclusion because time has run out. A missing conclusion costs marks in both Task Response and Coherence. If time is short, write a one-sentence conclusion.

Some people think that children should start formal schooling at a very early age, while others believe they should not begin until they are seven or older. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.

x: There is considerable disagreement about the right age for children to begin formal education. While some parents want their children in a classroom as early as possible, others feel that school should wait until around the age of seven. I believe a later start is generally better, provided young children still have access to good-quality play-based care.

Those who favour an early start argue that young children learn remarkably quickly and that this period should not be wasted. A four-year-old who is taught letters and numbers in a structured setting may enter primary school already able to read simple words, which gives a clear advantage over classmates. Early schooling can also help working parents, who would otherwise need to pay for private childcare, and it may give children from poorer homes a chance to catch up with wealthier peers.

On the other hand, many educators believe that formal lessons before seven do more harm than good. Children of this age learn best through play, conversation and exploring the world around them, and long periods of sitting still can make them associate learning with pressure. In Finland, where formal schooling begins at seven, students still perform among the best in Europe by their mid-teens, which suggests that a delayed start does not hold them back. I find this argument more convincing, because a child who enjoys learning at six is likely to keep enjoying it at sixteen.

In conclusion, although early schooling has some practical benefits, I believe children are better served by starting formal education at around seven, as long as the years before that are spent in a stimulating, play-based environment.
notes: The introduction paraphrases both views and states the writer's opinion clearly: 'I believe a later start is generally better'.
Body 1 explains the opposite view honestly (learning speed, working parents, poorer homes). It is not a straw man.
Body 2 combines view B with the writer's support: 'I find this argument more convincing'.
The Finland example is real and relevant, with no invented numbers.
The linkers sound natural: 'On the other hand', 'also', 'which suggests that'. There is no mechanical 'Firstly/Secondly' list.
The condition from the introduction (play-based care) returns in the conclusion, so the position stays consistent.

blocks.x: Below are sentences of the kind found in real student essays, each with a band 7+ version. Notice what has changed: more specific words, clearer logic and a link to the question.

x: Technology has many advantages and disadvantages for people in society.
Online banking saves customers a trip to the branch, but it also leaves older users more exposed to fraud.
Government should take steps to solve this problem.
The city authorities could introduce a congestion charge for private cars entering the centre during peak hours.
Students learn many things from studying abroad.
Living abroad forces students to manage their own budgets and solve everyday problems in a second language.
Crime is increasing day by day because of many reasons.
Youth crime tends to rise when unemployment among school leavers is high and few affordable activities are available.
People should do exercise because it is good for health.
Even thirty minutes of brisk walking a day lowers the risk of heart disease and type 2 diabetes.
Some people think this and some people think that.
Supporters of the policy point to its low cost, whereas critics question whether it would reach the people who need it most.
There are many causes of this problem. The first cause is money.
The main cause is financial: rents in central areas have risen much faster than wages.

blocks.q: Rewrite to band 7: 'Nowadays people use internet very much and it has good and bad effect.'
blocks.a: 'Most adults now spend several hours online every day, which has made information easier to access but has also reduced the time people spend talking face to face.'

blocks.q: Write a four-paragraph plan for this prompt: 'In many countries, traditional shops are closing as people shop online. What problems does this cause? What can be done?'
blocks.a: Intro: paraphrase + outline (loss of jobs and lively high streets; local incentives can help). Body 1 problems: job losses for shop staff, empty town centres, older people lose social contact. Body 2 solutions: lower business rates for small shops, turn empty units into cafes and community spaces, 'click and collect' partnerships. Conclusion: main problem + best solution in one sentence.

blocks.q: What is wrong with this conclusion? 'In conclusion, I agree with this statement. Also, governments should invest in new technology for the future.'
blocks.a: It brings a new idea (government investment in technology) into the conclusion and gives no reason for the position. A better version: 'In conclusion, I agree that ..., because ... and ....'

title: Coherence and cohesion
bn: Tie your ideas together: paragraphs, reference and linkers
goal: Here you will learn how to arrange paragraphs, how to refer back with this, such and these, how to use linkers correctly (and less often), and how to cut repetition with substitution.

pages.h: What examiners mean by coherence and cohesion

blocks.x: **Coherence** means the reader can follow your logic easily: the ideas come in a sensible order and every paragraph has one clear main idea. **Cohesion** means the sentences are joined through language: linkers, pronouns, reference words and substitution.

head: Band
Coherence and Cohesion in plain words
rows: Some organisation, but the progression is unclear; too few or too many linkers, or wrong ones; there may be no paragraphs
Overall progression is clear; linkers are used but are mechanical or faulty in places; reference is not always clear; there are paragraphs but they are not always logical
Logically organised with clear progression; a range of cohesive devices, with some under-use or over-use; each paragraph has a clear central topic
Information and ideas are sequenced, and every aspect of cohesion is well managed; paragraphing is sufficient and appropriate
Cohesion is so natural that it attracts no attention; paragraphing is skilful

blocks.x: Notice the word 'mechanical' in the band 6 descriptor. Starting every sentence with 'Firstly', 'In addition' or 'On the other hand' is exactly what it means. At band 7+ there are fewer linkers, but each one is in the right place.
Here is an easy test for your own essay: read only the first sentence of each paragraph. If those four or five sentences give the whole argument of the essay, your coherence is good.
One paragraph = one central idea. A new idea needs a new paragraph. Leave a blank line between paragraphs or indent them, but use the same style throughout the essay.

x: Four or five paragraphs: introduction, two or three body paragraphs, conclusion.
No one-sentence paragraphs (except the conclusion).
Do not mix two opposite ideas in one body paragraph unless you use a concession structure ('Although ..., ...').
Keep paragraphs roughly the same length. If one has 30 words and another 180, the essay is out of balance.

blocks.x: The **topic sentence** is the first line of a paragraph. It tells the reader what the paragraph is about. It should be general but not vague, and it should link to the question.

x: Firstly, there are many things to say about this.
The main argument for banning cars from city centres is the improvement in air quality.
On the other hand, some people have different opinions.
Shop owners, however, fear that a ban would keep customers away.
Secondly, money.
A second benefit of remote work is the money employees save on daily travel.
In my country, Bangladesh, my uncle works in an office.
Remote working is not suitable for every type of job.

blocks.x: If a body paragraph opens with an example ('For example, in 2019 ...'), the reader does not know what the example is supporting. Give the claim first, then the example.

blocks.q: Write a topic sentence for this paragraph: '... Buses and trains can carry far more people per square metre of road than private cars. If a city invests in fast, frequent services, many commuters will leave their cars at home, which reduces both congestion and emissions.'
blocks.a: 'Investing in public transport is the most effective way to reduce traffic in cities.'

pages.h: Referencing: this, these, such, it, they

blocks.x: A reference word points back to an earlier idea, so you do not have to repeat the noun. For band 7 your references must be clear: the reader should know at once what 'this' means.

head: Word
Refers to
Example
rows: 'Many graduates cannot find work. This problem is worst in rural areas.'
'Cars, buses and motorbikes all pollute. These vehicles ...'
'The policy was popular, but it was costly.'
The first / second of two things
'Cities and villages both grew, but the latter grew more slowly.'
'Old buses should be replaced with electric ones.'
'Students who want to work abroad should be allowed to do so.'

x: Many young people move to cities for jobs. This is bad.
Many young people move to cities for jobs. This trend leaves villages with an ageing population.
Parents and teachers should work together and they should talk to them more.
Parents and teachers should meet more often, and teachers should keep parents informed about their child's progress.
The government should build more hospitals and train more doctors. This will solve it.
The government should build more hospitals and train more doctors. Such investment would shorten waiting times considerably.

blocks.x: Do not write 'This' on its own. Write 'This + noun': 'This trend', 'This approach', 'This shift', 'This problem'. It makes the reference clear and shows your vocabulary too.
If 'they' could mean either of two plural nouns (parents and teachers), the reader gets confused. Repeat the noun or split the sentence.

pages.h: Linking words: used well and used badly

blocks.x: A linker shows the logic between sentences: contrast, cause, result. It does not create that logic. If the logic is missing, a linker cannot hide it.

head: Problem
Example
Fix
rows: 'Firstly, ... In addition, ... Also, ... On the other hand, ... However, ...' in every sentence
Two or three linkers per paragraph are enough; let the content connect the other sentences
'Cars pollute the air. Therefore, many people buy them.'
'Cars pollute the air. Even so, many people buy them for convenience.'
'However many people disagree.' / 'Although it is cheap, but it is slow.'
'However, many people disagree.' / 'Although it is cheap, it is slow.'
'Plus, ...', 'Also ...' at the start of many sentences, 'So, ...', 'Besides that, ...'
'On the contrary' means the previous statement is wrong; for a simple contrast use 'In contrast' or 'However'
'Last but not least', 'All in all, to sum up, in conclusion'

x: Firstly, online learning is cheap. Secondly, it is flexible. Thirdly, it is modern. In addition, students like it. Also it is popular.
Online learning is cheaper than campus study because students save on rent and travel. It is also flexible, which matters to those who work part time.
Pollution is increasing. On the other hand, governments should act.
Pollution is increasing, so governments need to act.
Although some people prefer cities. However I prefer villages.
Although some people prefer cities, I would rather live in a village.
Because many people cannot afford cars. So they use buses.
Because many people cannot afford cars, they rely on buses.

blocks.x: Use 'On the other hand' only when you are comparing two sides (on the one hand vs on the other hand). It is wrong when you are just adding a new point.

For variety, put some linkers in the middle of the sentence: 'This plan, however, would be expensive.' 'Many families, as a result, now rent rather than buy.' This makes your writing feel less mechanical.
The linkers below are grouped by function. Pay close attention to the grammar columns: some linkers start a sentence and take a comma, some join two clauses, and some come before a noun.

head: Function
Sentence start + comma
Joins two clauses
Before a noun / -ing
rows: In addition, / What is more, / Besides this,
However, / In contrast, / On the other hand,
For this reason, / This is because
because of / due to / owing to
As a result, / Therefore, / Consequently, / Thus,
in order to + verb / to + verb
if / unless / provided that / as long as
In other words, / That is to say,
In conclusion, / To sum up, / Overall,

x: Despite it is expensive, people buy it.
Despite its high price, people buy it. / Although it is expensive, people buy it.
Due to people are busy, they eat fast food.
Because people are busy, they eat fast food. / Due to their busy schedules, people eat fast food.
In spite of the fact the cost, ...
In spite of the cost, ... / In spite of the fact that it is costly, ...
Unless the government does not act, ...
Unless the government acts, ...

blocks.x: 'Despite' and 'due to' cannot be followed by a full clause (subject + verb). They need a noun or an -ing form. Otherwise use 'despite the fact that' or 'because'.
For band 7, knowing two or three options for each function is enough. Forcing in rare linkers such as 'notwithstanding' or 'hence' sounds unnatural.

Repeating the same noun again and again makes a text heavy. There are three ways to improve cohesion: pronouns and reference words, substitution (one, do so, the same), and **lexical chains** (words related to the topic, such as 'traffic, congestion, commuters, rush hour, vehicles').

x: Remote working saves time. Remote working also saves money. However, remote working can be lonely.
Remote working saves time and money. However, those who work from home can feel isolated, particularly if they live alone.
Some students like online classes. Other students do not like online classes.
Some students enjoy online classes, while others do not.
The government should ban plastic bags. If the government bans plastic bags, ...
The government should ban plastic bags. If it does so, ...
Old buses should be replaced with new buses.
Old buses should be replaced with electric ones.

head: Topic
A lexical chain you can move through
rows: traffic, congestion, gridlock, commuters, rush hour, private vehicles, road space
pollution, emissions, exhaust fumes, air quality, smog, contaminants
pupils, learners, the curriculum, classroom, lessons, academic performance
employees, staff, the workforce, employers, workplace, colleagues

blocks.x: Synonym cycling means writing 'children ... youngsters ... kids ... juveniles ... offspring' in one paragraph. It sounds strange. Repeating the main noun twice is fine, with a pronoun such as 'they' in between.

pages.h: A model essay with strong cohesion

blocks.x: More and more people are working from home rather than in an office. Do the advantages of this development outweigh the disadvantages?

x: Since 2020, a growing number of employees have swapped the office for their kitchen table, and many companies now let staff work remotely for at least part of the week. Although this shift has some real drawbacks, I believe its benefits are greater.

The main concern about remote work is its effect on relationships between colleagues. Much of what employees learn happens informally, by overhearing a conversation or asking a quick question at the next desk. When everyone is at home, these chances largely disappear, and new staff in particular may take longer to understand how their organisation works. Some people also find it hard to separate work from home life, especially if they live in small flats with no space for a desk.

These problems, however, are outweighed by the advantages. For many workers, the most obvious gain is time. A commuter in a congested city such as Dhaka can easily spend three hours a day travelling, and working from home returns that time for sleep, exercise or family. Employees also save money on transport and meals, which matters more as living costs rise. Employers benefit too: they can rent smaller offices and recruit talented people who live far from the city. What is more, fewer cars on the road during rush hour means less congestion and cleaner air for everyone.

Many of the drawbacks, in addition, can be reduced. Companies that bring teams together one or two days a week keep most of the social benefits of an office while still allowing staff to avoid daily travel.

In conclusion, although working from home can weaken team relationships, the time, money and environmental savings it brings make it a positive development, particularly when it is combined with regular face-to-face contact.
notes: You can follow the argument from the topic sentences alone: the concern, then 'These problems, however, are outweighed'.
'These problems' links the two paragraphs, and the reference is clear.
Linkers are few and varied (however, also, too, what is more, in addition), with no mechanical numbering.
'However' and 'in addition' sit in the middle of sentences, so the flow sounds natural.
Lexical chain: commute, travel, congestion, rush hour, cars.
The position (the benefits are greater) is consistent across the introduction, Body 2 and the conclusion.

blocks.q: Fix the linker: 'Many people like fast food. On the other hand, it is cheap.'
blocks.a: The logic is addition, not contrast: 'Many people like fast food, partly because it is cheap.' or 'Fast food is popular. It is also cheap.'

blocks.q: Use reference words to cut the repetition: 'The city built a new metro line. The new metro line has reduced traffic. The new metro line was expensive.'
blocks.a: 'The city built a new metro line. This has reduced traffic, although it was expensive to build.'

blocks.q: What is wrong? 'Although the policy is costly, but it is necessary.'
blocks.a: Do not use 'although' and 'but' together. 'Although the policy is costly, it is necessary.' or 'The policy is costly, but it is necessary.'

blocks.q: How many linkers can you remove from this paragraph? 'Firstly, exercise is good. Besides, it reduces stress. In addition, it helps sleep. Also, it is cheap.'
blocks.a: Almost all of them. Better: 'Regular exercise reduces stress and helps people sleep, and it costs almost nothing.' One sentence, with no mechanical linker.

blocks.q: Correct the 'despite' sentence: 'Despite he studied hard, he failed.'
blocks.a: 'Despite studying hard, he failed.' or 'Although he studied hard, he failed.'

blocks.q: Write a 'such + noun' sentence that follows this context: 'Some schools ban mobile phones during lessons.'
blocks.a: 'Such rules help students concentrate, although they can be hard to enforce.'

blocks.q: Write a sentence with 'the former / the latter'. Two options: building more roads, improving buses.
blocks.a: 'Cities can either build more roads or improve their bus networks; the latter is cheaper and does not encourage more car use.'

title: Grammar for band 7+
bn: You need range and accuracy: complex sentences done properly
goal: You will learn which complex structures you need for band 7+, how to keep punctuation and articles correct, and how to fix the 30 most common grammar mistakes made by Bangladeshi students.

pages.h: What Grammatical Range and Accuracy needs

blocks.x: This criterion covers two things: **range** (different kinds of sentence structure) and **accuracy** (how free of errors your writing is). If you only write simple sentences, your range is low. If your long, complicated sentences are full of mistakes, your accuracy is low.

head: Band
Range
Accuracy
rows: Limited range; attempts at complex sentences, but they are often inaccurate
Frequent errors and punctuation mistakes that make reading difficult
A mix of simple and complex
Some errors, but they rarely affect meaning
Frequent error-free sentences; good control of grammar and punctuation, though a few errors may remain
Most sentences are error-free; occasional non-systematic errors

blocks.x: The magic phrase for band 7 is 'frequent error-free sentences'. This means most of your sentences should contain no mistakes at all. So using common complex structures accurately is worth more than forcing in rare ones.

Keep a mix in every paragraph: one short, clear sentence and one or two complex sentences (a relative clause, a conditional or a concession). A paragraph of four 40-word sentences has a much higher chance of errors.
A systematic error (the same mistake again and again, such as dropping the 's' on every plural) tells the examiner that you do not know the rule. It costs more marks than an occasional slip.
A **relative clause** (who, which, that, where, whose) lets you combine two sentences into one and define a noun. A band 7 essay has one in almost every paragraph.

head: Type
Example
Comma?
rows: 'Students who work part time often have less time to study.'
'Dhaka, which has over 20 million residents, suffers from severe congestion.'
'Families whose income is low cannot afford private tutors.'
'Cities where public transport is cheap have fewer cars.'
'Many graduates move abroad, which weakens the local economy.'
'People living in rural areas' (= who live), 'Goods made locally' (= which are made)

x: Many people live in cities. They suffer from noise.
Many people who live in cities suffer from constant noise.
The teacher which taught me was strict.
The teacher who taught me was strict.
Dhaka which is the capital is very crowded.
Dhaka, which is the capital, is extremely crowded.
Many young people leave villages. This is a problem for farming.
Many young people leave villages, which creates a labour shortage on farms.

blocks.x: The **noun phrase** is a strength of academic writing: you express an idea with a noun instead of a verb. This sounds formal and dense.

x: Because cities are growing fast, ...
The rapid growth of cities ...
If we use fewer cars, ...
A reduction in car use ...
When people do not have enough money, ...
A lack of financial resources ...
Governments are spending more on health.
Government spending on health has increased.

blocks.x: 'That' cannot introduce a non-defining clause (after a comma): 'Dhaka, that is crowded, ...' is wrong. After a comma, use 'which' or 'who'.
In a Task 2 essay you need conditionals to propose solutions, make predictions and argue about hypothetical situations. Knowing three forms is enough.

head: Form
Use in essays
Example
rows: 'If children sleep less, they concentrate less.'
Real possible result of a policy
'If the city builds a metro, traffic will fall.'
'If university were free, more poor students would apply.'
unless, provided that, as long as, otherwise
'The scheme will fail unless it is properly funded.'

x: If government will reduce tax, people will buy more.
If the government reduces tax, people will buy more.
If I was the president, I will ban plastic.
If I were in charge, I would ban single-use plastic.
Unless the government does not act, pollution will rise.
Unless the government acts, pollution will rise.

blocks.x: Use the **passive** when the action matters more than who does it, or when everyone knows who does it. It sounds natural in academic writing.

x: People should teach children about money at school.
Children should be taught about money at school.
They built many factories near the river.
Many factories were built near the river.
Someone must do something about this.
Action must be taken to address this.
The problem is happened because of traffic.
The problem is caused by traffic. / The problem happens because of traffic.

blocks.x: Intransitive verbs (happen, occur, arise, increase in the sense of 'go up', die, remain) have no passive form: 'It is happened' is wrong; 'It happened' or 'It has happened' is right.
A **participle clause** (starting with an -ing or -ed form) joins two ideas in a shorter way. The subject must be the same in both parts, or you get a 'dangling' error.

x: People work from home. They save travel time.
Working from home, people save travel time.
The policy was introduced in 2015. It has cut emissions.
Introduced in 2015, the policy has cut emissions.
Walking to the office, the rain started.
While I was walking to the office, it started to rain.

blocks.x: **Concession** means accepting an opposing point before making your own. It is very useful for band 7+ arguments because it shows balanced thinking.

head: Structure
Example
rows: 'Although online courses are cheaper, they require strong self-discipline.'
'While some argue that zoos are cruel, many protect endangered species.'
'Despite its cost, the metro has been a success.'
'Admittedly, the scheme is expensive. However, the long-term savings are considerable.'
'Useful as social media is, it can spread false information quickly.'

blocks.x: Use **inversion** rarely, at most once in an essay. No inversion is better than a wrong inversion.

x: People rarely consider the environmental cost.
Rarely do people consider the environmental cost.
People will not only save money, they will also save time.
Not only will people save money, but they will also save time.
If the government had acted earlier, ...
Had the government acted earlier, ...

blocks.x: When a sentence starts with 'Not only', the auxiliary comes first: 'Not only it saves money' is wrong; 'Not only does it save money' is right.

Punctuation mistakes count directly against GRA. The two most common are the **comma splice** (two full sentences joined with a comma) and the **fragment** (half a sentence written as if it were a full one).

head: Error
Wrong
Right
rows: 'Technology is useful because it saves time.' / 'Technology is useful; it saves time.'
'Many people choose it because it is cheap.'
'However many people disagree.' / 'If prices rise people buy less.'
'However, many people disagree.' / 'If prices rise, people buy less.'
'Some argue, that cars should be banned.'
'Some argue that cars should be banned.'
'People are busy they eat fast food.'
'People are busy, so they eat fast food.'

x: A semicolon (;) joins two closely related full sentences, but once or twice in an essay is enough.
A colon (:) is followed by an explanation or a list: 'The cause is simple: rents have risen faster than wages.'
Avoid contractions (don't, can't, it's) in a formal essay: write 'do not', 'cannot', 'it is'.
Avoid exclamation marks (!) and rhetorical questions in your essay.

blocks.q: Fix the comma splice: 'Many students study abroad, they want better jobs.'
blocks.a: 'Many students study abroad because they want better jobs.' or 'Many students study abroad; they hope to find better jobs.'

blocks.x: Bangla has no direct equivalent of 'a/an/the', so articles cause more mistakes for Bangladeshi students than anything else. The main rules are below.

head: Rule
Example
rows: A singular countable noun cannot stand alone
'A car is expensive.' / 'The car ...' / 'Cars are ...' (not 'Car is expensive')
'The pollution in Dhaka is severe.' 'the government' (your country's)
Country names: no 'the' unless plural or 'Republic/Kingdom'
a vs an: depends on the sound

blocks.x: **Subject-verb agreement**: find the main subject and ignore the phrase in the middle.

x: The number of cars are increasing.
The number of cars is increasing.
One of the main problem are pollution.
One of the main problems is pollution.
Everyone have a smartphone.
Everyone has a smartphone.
The use of mobile phones in schools have increased.
The use of mobile phones in schools has increased.
People who lives in cities ...
People who live in cities ...
A lot of information are available.
A lot of information is available.

blocks.x: Uncountable nouns have no plural and do not take 'a': information, advice, equipment, furniture, knowledge (in general), research, evidence, traffic, homework, luggage, news (with a singular verb).

blocks.q: Correct the articles: 'Government should invest in education because education is key to the development of country.'
blocks.a: 'The government should invest in education because education is key to a country's development.'

pages.h: The 30 most common errors of Bangladeshi students

blocks.x: This list comes from real essays by Bangladeshi students. Compare it with your last three essays and find out which of these are your 'systematic' errors.

head: Wrong
Right
Why
rows: 'agree' is a verb, so you do not need 'am'
'according to' is for other people's views
do not use although and but together
Despite the cost / In spite of the cost
It is useful, it saves time.
It is useful because it saves time.
He suggested that I study. / He advised me to study.
It makes them to work hard.
They lack money. / They have a lack of money.

blocks.x: Write your own top five mistakes from these 30 on a card. In the last five minutes of the exam, look only for those five.

pages.h: A model essay with a wide grammatical range

blocks.x: In many cities, young people are finding it increasingly difficult to afford a place to live. What are the causes of this problem, and what measures could be taken to solve it?

x: In many large cities, young adults now spend such a high share of their income on rent that buying a home seems out of reach. This essay argues that the problem stems mainly from a shortage of new housing and from property being treated as an investment, and that both causes can be addressed by government action.

The most obvious cause is that housing supply has not kept pace with demand. As jobs become concentrated in a few major cities, people move there in large numbers, but planning rules and slow approval processes mean that new flats take years to build. When demand rises faster than supply, prices inevitably climb. A second factor is that property has become a popular investment. Wealthy individuals, some of whom live abroad, buy flats not to live in but to rent out or simply to hold as their value increases. This pushes prices beyond what a young teacher or nurse, earning an ordinary salary, could ever hope to pay.

Several measures could ease the situation. Had governments reformed planning laws earlier, many cities would already have far more affordable homes, so simplifying approvals for medium-sized apartment blocks near public transport should be a priority. Authorities could also build social housing that is rented at a fixed share of tenants' income, as Vienna has done successfully for decades. Finally, higher taxes on homes that are left empty, or on second properties owned purely for profit, would discourage speculation and could fund new construction.

In conclusion, young people are being priced out of cities largely because too few homes are built and too many are bought as investments. If governments increased supply and made speculation less attractive, housing would become noticeably more affordable within a decade.
notes: Relative clauses: 'some of whom live abroad', 'that is rented at a fixed share'.
Conditionals: zero ('When demand rises ...'), second ('If governments increased ...') and one inversion ('Had governments reformed ...'), used only once.
The passive sounds natural: 'are being priced out', 'are bought as investments', 'is rented'.
Noun phrases: 'a shortage of new housing', 'simplifying approvals for medium-sized apartment blocks'.
Participle phrase: 'earning an ordinary salary' makes the meaning compact.
Articles, plurals and agreement are correct throughout, so the complex structures do not cost accuracy.

blocks.q: Join with a relative clause: 'Many farmers grow rice. Their land is flooded every year.'
blocks.a: 'Many farmers whose land is flooded every year still grow rice.'

blocks.q: Write a second conditional: free public transport, fewer cars.
blocks.a: 'If public transport were free, fewer people would drive to work.'

blocks.q: Make it passive: 'The authorities closed three factories last year.'
blocks.a: 'Three factories were closed last year.'

blocks.q: Write one sentence with a concession: social media connects people / spreads false news.
blocks.a: 'Although social media connects people across the world, it also allows false news to spread rapidly.'

blocks.q: Find the errors: 'Nowadays the peoples are more depend on technology, it make them lazy.'
blocks.a: 'Nowadays people depend more on technology, which makes them lazy.' (peoples, 'the', are depend, comma splice, make/makes)

blocks.q: Fill in the articles: '___ internet has changed ___ way ___ students learn, but ___ access is still limited in ___ rural areas.'
blocks.a: 'The internet has changed the way students learn, but access is still limited in rural areas.' (The last three gaps need no article.)

goal: The aim of this chapter is to teach you collocations, ways to avoid repetition, how to choose precise and formal words, and a ready vocabulary bank for ten common topics.

pages.h: What Lexical Resource needs, and collocations

blocks.x: The band 7 descriptor mentions a 'sufficient range of vocabulary to allow some flexibility and precision' and says the writer 'uses less common lexical items with some awareness of style and collocation'. blocks.x: A **collocation** is a group of words that native speakers naturally use together. 'Make a decision' is right; 'do a decision' is wrong. Collocations are the quickest way for an examiner to judge whether your vocabulary sounds natural.

pages.h: A model essay and vocabulary checks

blocks.x: Many people today prefer to buy imported food rather than local produce. Why is this the case? Is this a positive or negative development?

x: In many countries, supermarket shelves are now filled with fruit, cheese and snacks flown in from other continents, and a large number of shoppers choose these over locally grown food. This essay explains why imported products have become so popular and argues that, on balance, the trend is a negative one.

Several factors explain this preference. Imported food is often perceived as higher in quality or safer, particularly in countries where local food safety standards are weakly enforced. Price also matters: large agricultural producers abroad benefit from economies of scale, so their goods can be cheaper than those of small local farmers, even after transport costs. In addition, global advertising and travel have changed tastes, and many middle-class consumers now associate foreign brands with a modern lifestyle.

Although consumers gain more choice, I believe the wider consequences are mostly harmful. The first concern is environmental. Food that is transported thousands of kilometres by air or refrigerated ship generates far higher carbon emissions than produce bought from a nearby market. The second is economic. When shoppers turn away from local produce, small farmers lose income, and rural communities that depend on agriculture may decline as young people leave in search of work. Finally, a heavy reliance on imports makes a country vulnerable: if global supply chains are disrupted, as they were during the pandemic, prices can rise sharply overnight.

In conclusion, people buy imported food mainly because they trust its quality, find it affordable and are drawn to foreign brands. While this gives consumers a wider choice, its environmental and economic costs mean that it is, overall, a negative development.
notes: Topic collocations sound natural: 'food safety standards', 'economies of scale', 'carbon emissions', 'supply chains'.
There is no repetition: imported food, foreign brands, these products and imports are each chosen to suit the context.
Precise words: 'weakly enforced', 'vulnerable', 'disrupted'. There is no vague 'bad' or 'big'.
The register is formal but natural, with no memorised cliches.
Both parts of the two-part prompt are answered: the reasons (Body 1) and the negative judgement (Body 2 and the conclusion).
The hedging is accurate ('often perceived', 'may decline'), and there is no over-generalisation.

title: Opinion essays (agree or disagree)
bn: How far do you agree? Take a clear position and hold it to the end
goal: In this chapter you will learn how to answer an agree/disagree question by taking a clear position, planning your essay and writing it at band 8 level.

blocks.x: In an opinion essay, IELTS gives you a statement and asks how far you agree with it. The examiner's main question is simple: did you take **a clear position** and keep it through the whole essay?

x: 'To what extent do you agree or disagree?'
'Do you agree or disagree?'
'What is your opinion?'
'Do you think this is a good idea?' / 'Is this a fair policy?'

blocks.x: All of these wordings ask for the same thing: your view on the statement, your reasons and your examples. 'To what extent' means you may fully agree, fully disagree or partly agree. Any of these is fine as long as it is clear.

head: Position
Thesis example
When to choose it
rows: 'I fully agree that public transport deserves more funding than roads.'
When you can easily find 2 strong reasons for one side
'I disagree. Online learning cannot replace classrooms.'
'I largely agree, although roads are still needed in rural areas.'
When one side is strong but has a clear limit

blocks.x: For band 7, the Task Response descriptor says 'presents a clear position throughout the response'. At band 6 there is a position, but the conclusion 'may become unclear or repetitive'. So keeping your position clear is the cheapest way to move from 6 to 7.
Choose the side where you can quickly find 2 strong ideas and examples. The examiner does not check your 'real' belief. The examiner checks how good your argument is.
Ending the essay with 'Both sides have good points, so it depends'. That is not an answer. Even if you partly agree, you must say which side you lean towards and why.
A 4 or 5 paragraph structure is the safest choice for an opinion essay. Learn the table below by heart and you will be able to plan in 5 minutes in the exam hall.

x: Shape A (full agree/disagree): Intro > Reason 1 > Reason 2 > Conclusion
Shape B (largely agree): Intro > Reason 1 > Reason 2 > Limit/concession > Conclusion
Shape C (balanced but clear): Intro > Opposite view + rebuttal > Your reason(s) > Conclusion
Minutes 0-2: Read the question twice and underline the keywords.
Minutes 2-5: Decide your position. Note down 2 reasons and one example for each.
Minutes 5-35: Write. Spend 4 minutes on the introduction, 9-10 minutes on each body paragraph and 3 minutes on the conclusion.
Minutes 35-40: Check articles, subject-verb agreement, plurals and spelling.

blocks.x: Use the PEEL formula for body paragraphs: Point (topic sentence), Explain (why), Example (specific), Link (back to your position). Check that every body paragraph has all four.

Some people think that governments should spend money on public transport rather than on building new roads. To what extent do you agree or disagree?

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

Write at least 250 words.

x: Pick out the keywords: 'governments', 'spend money', 'public transport', 'rather than', 'new roads'. 'Rather than' signals a comparison, so you must compare the two. Praising public transport alone is not enough.
Decide your position: public transport is the better choice, but villages still need roads. So you 'largely agree'.
Brainstorm for 2 minutes (see the list below).
Choose the 2 strongest reasons: (1) space and capacity, (2) the environment and fairness. Concession: rural roads.
Find a specific example for each reason: the Dhaka metro compared with flyovers.
Write the thesis first, then the body paragraphs, and finally the conclusion.

For roads: villages have few passengers; goods move by lorry; buses also need roads
Example bank: Dhaka metro (Uttara to Motijheel under 40 min), flyovers moving jams, air pollution in Dhaka

blocks.x: Here is the full essay written from the plan. Notice which job from the table each paragraph is doing.

x: As cities grow, traffic gets worse every year, and governments have to decide where limited transport budgets should go. Some people argue that this money is better spent on buses, trains and trams than on new roads. I largely agree, although some road building will always be necessary, especially outside large cities.

The main reason I support public transport is that it moves far more people in far less space. One metro line can carry tens of thousands of passengers an hour, while a new highway lane often fills with cars within a few years, because better roads encourage more people to drive. Dhaka shows this clearly. Several flyovers built to ease congestion have mostly moved traffic jams from one junction to the next, yet the metro now takes passengers from Uttara to Motijheel in under forty minutes, a trip that can take two hours by road.

Public transport also brings wider benefits that roads cannot match. Per passenger, buses and trains produce far lower emissions than private cars, which matters in cities where polluted air is already a serious health risk. It is also fairer. Students, older people and low-income workers who cannot afford a car depend on public services to reach jobs, schools and hospitals, whereas money spent on roads mainly helps those who already own vehicles.

That said, roads cannot be ignored entirely. Rural areas rarely have enough passengers to justify a railway, and farm produce and factory goods still have to reach markets by lorry. In such places, building and repairing roads remains a sensible use of public money.

On balance, I believe most transport spending in cities should go to public transport, since it carries more people, pollutes less and serves those without cars. New roads still have a role, but mainly in rural regions where there is no realistic alternative.
notes: The last line of the introduction makes the position clear: 'I largely agree, although...'. From the first paragraph, the examiner knows where you stand.

In Body 1 the claim comes with a reason ('because better roads encourage more people to drive'), followed by a specific local example (the Dhaka metro, Uttara to Motijheel). It avoids a vague example such as 'in many countries'.
Body 3 ('That said...') is the concession. It supports the 'largely agree' position. It does not change it.
The linking is natural: 'That said', 'whereas', 'On balance'. There is no mechanical chain of 'Firstly... Secondly... Also' anywhere.
The vocabulary is precise: 'justify a railway', 'low-income workers', 'realistic alternative', 'per passenger'. These are accurate words, not fancy ones.
The conclusion adds no new ideas. It restates the position and the main reasons in different words.

pages.h: Model essay 2: disagreeing with an extreme claim

blocks.x: When a statement contains extreme words such as 'eventually replace', 'always' or 'only', disagreeing is easy. A single good exception is enough to break the claim.

Some people believe that online learning will eventually replace traditional classrooms in schools and universities. To what extent do you agree or disagree?

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

Write at least 250 words.

x: Thesis: Disagree, online learning is a supplement, not a replacement
Body 1: young students need supervision; pandemic experience
Body 2: school teaches social and practical skills; lab, medical training
Body 3 (concession): good for working adults and remote students
Conclusion: classrooms stay at the centre, delivery may change

Since the pandemic, online courses and video lectures have become a normal part of education, and some people now predict that physical classrooms will soon disappear. I disagree. While online learning is a useful addition, I do not believe it can replace schools and universities, mainly because learning depends on people as much as on information.

The first problem is that most students, especially younger ones, need structure and supervision. In a classroom, a teacher can see when a child has stopped listening or has misunderstood a step, and can respond immediately. At home in front of a laptop, the same child can open a game in seconds. When schools closed during the pandemic, many parents discovered how hard it was to keep children focused on lessons through a screen, and the students who were already struggling usually fell furthest behind.

Secondly, school is about more than passing exams. Students learn to work in teams, disagree politely and make friends from different backgrounds, and these skills grow through daily contact rather than through a chat window. Practical subjects make the point even clearer: a chemistry student needs a real laboratory, and a medical student cannot learn to examine patients from a recorded video.

There are, of course, situations where online learning works very well. Adults with full-time jobs can take evening courses that fit their schedules, and students in remote villages can watch lectures from top universities. However, these advantages make online study a valuable supplement, not a replacement.

For these reasons, I think classrooms will remain at the centre of education. Technology will probably change how lessons are delivered, but the supervision, social contact and hands-on practice that schools provide cannot be moved fully online.
notes: A short, strong thesis: 'I disagree.' It is followed by a one-line preview of the main reason: 'learning depends on people as much as on information'.
Body 1 develops the idea through contrast: in a classroom the teacher can see the child, while at home on a laptop the child opens a game. The examiner can picture the scene.
The examples in Body 2 are very concrete: a chemistry lab, medical students examining patients. They give the abstract claim some proof.
The opposite side is not ignored (P4), but the phrase 'supplement, not a replacement' folds it into your own position.
Grammar range: a relative clause ('students who were already struggling'), a passive ('cannot be moved') and a modal ('can respond'). They all appear naturally.

blocks.x: End the concession paragraph by returning to your position: 'However, these advantages make it a supplement, not a replacement.' If you skip this, the examiner may think you have changed sides.

pages.h: A band 6 version and why it stays at 6

blocks.x: Here is a typical band 6 essay on the same prompt (public transport). The ideas are almost the same, but the score is 2 bands lower. Read the comments to see why.

x: Nowadays traffic jam is a very big problem in all over the world. Some people think government should spend money for public transport instead of building new roads. In this essay I will discuss about this topic and give my opinion.

Firstly, public transport is very important for people. Many people use bus and train every day to go to their office. If government spend more money on public transport, then people will get more facilities. It saves time for the office workers and students. For example, in my country metro rail is very helpful for the people. Also, public transport is good for environment because it reduces pollution. So government should give more money for public transport.

Secondly, new roads are also important. Without roads, people cannot go from one place to another place. In village areas there are many bad roads and people face many problems. Besides, trucks need roads to carry goods to the market. So roads are also necessary for the development of the country and we cannot ignore it.

On the other hand, if government build more roads, more people will buy cars and the traffic jam will increase more. This is a big problem in big cities like Dhaka. People waste many hours in traffic jam every day and they become tired and frustrated. Even the new flyovers could not solve this problem.

To conclude, both public transport and roads are important for a country. Government should spend money on both of them. But I think public transport is more important because it helps many people and it is good for environment.
notes: Task Response 6: the position only appears at the end. Body 2 argues for roads, and the conclusion says 'both important' and then 'public transport more important'. The position is never clear, which is the classic sign of band 6.
The ideas are there but not developed: 'metro rail is very helpful for the people'. Helpful in what way? How much time does it save? There is no detail, so the example stays distant and does no work.
Coherence 6: P4 begins with 'On the other hand', but P4 actually argues for public transport. A linker in the wrong place breaks the logic for the examiner.
Lexical 6: 'people', 'traffic jam', 'important' and 'problem' are repeated again and again. 'more facilities' and 'face many problems' are very general.

Grammar 6: 'government spend', 'discuss about', 'in all over the world', 'good for environment' (article missing), 'ignore it' (roads is plural). The meaning is clear, so it gets 6, but the errors are frequent.
'In this essay I will discuss about this topic' gives no information. A clear thesis in place of this line would lift the introduction to 7+.

Some people think that children should be taught to compete at school, while others believe it is more important to teach them to cooperate.

Discuss both these views and give your own opinion.

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

Write at least 250 words.

x: Paraphrase the two views: View A = compete (rivalry, winning). View B = cooperate (teamwork, sharing).
Brainstorm A: the real world is competitive (jobs, scholarships), motivation. Example: a science fair.
Brainstorm B: jobs need teamwork, ranking makes kids hide knowledge, group projects. Example: engineers, doctors.
Opinion: cooperation matters more, but competition stays as a source of motivation. Reason: competition rewards only the top few.
Order: View A (competition) first, because your side is B.
Both views have their own advantages and I will discuss both of them.
Both have value, but in my view cooperation deserves more emphasis.
Some people think competition is good.
Those who favour competition argue that it reflects the real world.
In my opinion both are important.
I find the second argument more convincing.

Schools prepare children for adult life, but people disagree about which attitude matters more: the drive to compete or the ability to cooperate. Both have value, but in my view cooperation deserves more emphasis, with competition kept in its place as a source of motivation.

Those who favour competition argue that it reflects the real world. Students will later compete for university places, scholarships and jobs, so learning to handle rivalry early may make them more resilient. Competition can also push children to work harder than they otherwise would. A student who knows that the best science project will be shown at a national fair, for instance, is likely to spend extra evenings improving it. From this point of view, removing competition from schools would leave young people unprepared for pressure.

Supporters of cooperation, however, point out that almost every modern job depends on teamwork. Engineers, doctors and software developers rarely succeed alone; they need to share information, divide tasks and settle disagreements. Children who are constantly ranked against their classmates may learn to hide what they know rather than share it. Group projects, by contrast, teach students to listen, to explain ideas clearly and to take responsibility for a shared result.

I find the second argument more convincing. Competition tends to reward only the top few students, while those who regularly come last may lose confidence and stop trying altogether. Cooperation helps every child, including the weakest, because each member of a team has a role to play. Healthy competition can still exist, for example in sports or quizzes, but it should not become the main way schools judge children.
All things considered, competition is useful as a motivator, but learning to work with others is the more valuable lesson for children to carry from school into adult life.
notes: The introduction paraphrases both views ('the drive to compete or the ability to cooperate') and gives the opinion straight away: 'cooperation deserves more emphasis'. Giving your opinion in the introduction makes TR stronger in a discussion essay too.
Body 1 and Body 2 are both fair: each view is presented with its strongest reason and example. The examiner can see that you have really discussed 'both views'.
Body 1 uses 'those who favour...' and Body 2 uses 'supporters of... argue'. This distancing language shows that these are other people's views, not your opinion.
The opinion gets its own paragraph (P4), which explains why one view is more convincing: 'rewards only the top few'. Simply saying 'I agree with the second view' would not have been enough.
Varied linking: 'however', 'by contrast', 'From this point of view', 'All things considered'. There is not a single 'On the other hand', yet the contrast is clear.

blocks.x: Notice that the model essay uses 'I' only in the introduction, P4 and the conclusion. Body 1 and Body 2 contain no opinion. This separation shows the examiner the three parts of the task clearly.

Some people believe that the best way to reduce crime is to give longer prison sentences. Others, however, think there are better alternative ways of reducing crime.

Discuss both these views and give your own opinion.

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

Write at least 250 words.

x: View A (longer sentences): protects public, deters crime, justice for serious crimes
View B (alternatives): prison creates more criminals, alternatives tackle causes (poverty, addiction, skills)
My opinion: B, but long sentences for dangerous offenders
Example: Norway's rehabilitation system and low reoffending

Governments everywhere want to cut crime, but there is little agreement on how to do it. Some believe that longer prison sentences are the answer, while others argue that money is better spent on prevention and rehabilitation. Although harsh punishment has some role, I believe the second approach is more effective.

People who support longer sentences usually make two points. First, an offender who is in prison cannot harm the public, so keeping dangerous criminals locked up for longer directly protects communities. Second, the threat of a long sentence may discourage people from breaking the law in the first place. For serious violent crimes such as armed robbery or murder, many also feel that a long sentence is simply what justice requires.

Critics, however, argue that prison often makes the problem worse. Inmates, especially young people convicted of minor offences, may spend years alongside experienced criminals and leave with fewer job prospects and stronger criminal contacts. This helps explain why so many former prisoners reoffend. These critics prefer alternatives such as community service, drug treatment and education inside prisons, which deal with the reasons people turn to crime, including poverty, addiction and a lack of skills.

In my opinion, the evidence supports this second view. Norway, for example, focuses on rehabilitation rather than long sentences, and its reoffending rate is among the lowest in Europe. Long sentences should be kept for offenders who pose a real danger to others, but for most crimes, training and treatment protect society better in the long run.
For these reasons, I believe that while prison is necessary for the most dangerous criminals, crime is reduced more effectively by tackling its causes than by simply extending punishment.
notes: The thesis adds some balance with 'Although harsh punishment has some role', but the final view is clear: 'the second approach is more effective'.
Body 1 makes two points with 'First... Second...', and each has a why. Simple list linking is natural here because it stays inside one paragraph.
Body 2 has a cause and effect chain: young offender > experienced criminals > fewer job prospects > reoffending. This is development, not just a list.
The opinion paragraph supports the opinion with a real example (Norway, low reoffending). It gives no number, but the fact is accurate.
Topic-specific vocabulary appears naturally: 'reoffend', 'rehabilitation', 'convicted of minor offences', 'pose a real danger'.

x: Nowadays education is very important for children. Some people think children should learn competition in school but other people think cooperation is more important. Both views have their own advantages and I will discuss both of them in this essay.

Some people believe that competition is good for children. Because in the future they have to compete for job and university admission. If they learn competition from childhood, they will become strong and confident. Also, competition make students work hard. For example, when there is exam, students study more for getting good marks. Many parents also want their children to be first in the class. So competition is very necessary for the students.

Other people believe that cooperation is more important. In the office, people have to work with team. If children learn cooperation in school, they can work with others easily when they get a job. Teamwork is very important in modern world and they will need this skill in every job. In addition, cooperation helps children to make friends and they can share their knowledge with each other. For example, group study is very helpful for students.

In my opinion, both competition and cooperation are important for children. Competition helps students to do better and cooperation helps them to work together. Teachers should teach both of them in school so that children can become successful in their life. Without these two things, children cannot do well.
Finally I want to say that competition and cooperation both have advantages and disadvantages. Schools should give importance to both of them for a better future of children.

In many countries, more people are now working from home rather than travelling to an office every day.

Do the advantages of this trend outweigh the disadvantages?

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

Write at least 250 words.

x: Version: 'Do the advantages outweigh' = an opinion is required.
Advantages brainstorm: no commute, save money, better focus, companies save rent, hire from anywhere.
Disadvantages brainstorm: isolation, work-life line blurs, juniors learn less, poor home internet.
Judgement: the advantages are greater. Weighing reason: the problems are manageable (hybrid work), but time lost to commuting can never be recovered.
Example: a 2-3 hour commute in Dhaka; a hybrid model with 2-3 days in the office.
This trend has many advantages and disadvantages which I will discuss.
Although working from home has some real drawbacks, I believe its benefits are greater.
Firstly, people can save their time.
The most obvious advantage is the time saved on commuting.
In my opinion, it has both advantages and disadvantages.
In my view, these problems are real but manageable.

Remote work, once rare, has become common in many countries since 2020, particularly in fields such as software, marketing and finance. Although working from home has some real drawbacks, I believe its benefits are greater, both for employees and for the companies that employ them.

The most obvious advantage is the time saved on commuting. In a city like Dhaka, an office worker can easily spend two or three hours a day in traffic, and working from home turns that time into extra rest, family time or study. It also cuts spending on transport and meals. Many employees find they concentrate better at home, away from the noise of an open-plan office. For companies, remote teams mean smaller offices and lower rent, and they can hire skilled people who live in other cities or even other countries.

There are, however, genuine disadvantages. Some employees feel isolated without colleagues around them, and the line between work and private life can blur when the laptop never leaves the kitchen table. Junior staff may suffer most, as they miss the informal learning that comes from watching experienced colleagues deal with problems. Besides, not everyone has a quiet room or a reliable internet connection at home.

In my view, these problems are real but manageable. Many firms now use a hybrid model, in which staff come to the office two or three days a week for meetings and training and work from home for the rest. This keeps most of the benefits while reducing isolation and giving new employees time with mentors. The hours lost in commuting, by contrast, can never be recovered.
For these reasons, I believe the advantages of working from home outweigh the disadvantages, particularly when it is combined with regular days in the office.
notes: An 'outweigh' question needs an opinion. The last line of the introduction makes it clear: 'I believe its benefits are greater'.
The advantages paragraph covers two angles, the employee and the company, in a single paragraph. This keeps the essay balanced without making it too long.
The disadvantages paragraph is fair: 'genuine disadvantages', 'Junior staff may suffer most'. The examiner sees that you are taking the other side seriously.
P4 is the 'weighing' paragraph: it explains why the advantages are greater (the problems are manageable, and commuting time cannot be recovered). This paragraph is the heart of an 'outweigh' essay.
Specific detail: 'two or three hours a day in traffic', 'two or three days a week'. Concrete numbers make the essay feel real.

blocks.x: This prompt has no 'outweigh'. It only asks 'What are the advantages and disadvantages', so the essay is balanced. Notice how every point is tied to 'for the students themselves'.

An increasing number of students are choosing to study at universities in other countries.

What are the advantages and disadvantages of this for the students themselves?

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

Write at least 250 words.

x: Advantages (academic): better facilities, valued degree, faster language learning
Advantages (personal): independence, international contacts
Disadvantages: cost, loneliness/homesickness, recognition at home
Conclusion: summary + 'weigh carefully'

Each year, more young people leave their home countries to study abroad, with the UK, Canada, Australia and Germany among the most popular destinations. This choice can bring students clear academic and personal benefits, but it also involves heavy financial and emotional costs.

The first advantage is access to teaching and facilities that may not be available at home. Many foreign universities have better-equipped laboratories, smaller classes and close links with industry, and a degree from a well-known institution can make a graduate more attractive to employers. Students also improve their English or another foreign language far faster when they use it every day for lectures, shopping and friendship than they would in a classroom at home.

Living abroad also builds independence. A student who must manage a budget, cook, find accommodation and handle official paperwork alone soon becomes more mature and confident. Classmates from many countries widen their view of the world and may become useful contacts later in their careers.

On the other hand, studying abroad is extremely expensive. Even with a partial scholarship, tuition and living costs in cities such as London or Toronto can place a heavy burden on a family, and some students take part-time jobs that leave them too tired to study properly. Loneliness is another serious problem. Far from family and friends, and facing a new climate, food and culture, many international students struggle with homesickness, especially in their first year. Finally, a foreign qualification is not always fully recognised at home, which can make returning difficult.

In short, studying abroad offers a better education, stronger language skills and personal growth, but students need to weigh these gains carefully against the high cost and the strain of living far from home.
notes: This prompt does not ask for an opinion ('What are the advantages and disadvantages'), so the essay is balanced and has no 'I believe'. The conclusion gives only a practical summary.
The prompt says 'for the students themselves'. Every point in the essay is about the student's life, not about the country or the university. This detail matters a great deal for TR.
There are 2 paragraphs of advantages (academic, personal) and 1 long paragraph of disadvantages. Balance is measured in word count, not in paragraph count.
The disadvantages paragraph has 3 points ('expensive', 'Loneliness', 'Finally, ... not always recognised'), and each one is explained. It is not just a list.
Natural collocations: 'place a heavy burden on', 'struggle with homesickness', 'widen their view', 'weigh these gains against'.

x: In recent years, working from home has become very popular in many countries. Many people now work from their house instead of going to office. This trend has many advantages and disadvantages which I will discuss in this essay.

There are many advantages of working from home. Firstly, people can save their time because they do not need to go to office. In Dhaka city traffic jam is very bad, so it is a big advantage. Secondly, people can save money. They do not need to pay for bus or rickshaw. Thirdly, they can spend more time with family. They can also wake up later and feel more relaxed. So working from home has many advantages for the employees.

However, there are also some disadvantages. Firstly, people can feel lonely because they cannot meet their colleagues. Secondly, sometimes internet connection is not good in home and they cannot do their work properly. Sometimes there is also load shedding in our country. Thirdly, some people cannot focus on work in home because of family members and children. Also, the boss cannot check if the employee is working or not.

In my opinion, working from home has both advantages and disadvantages. It depends on the person and the job. Some people like to work from home and some people like to work in office. Companies should give option to the employees.
To conclude, working from home is a good thing but it has also some problems. If companies and employees can solve the problems, then working from home will be more beneficial in the future.
