blocks.x:
In many countries, the number of overweight children is increasing.

What are the causes of this problem, and what measures could be taken to solve it?

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

Write at least 250 words.

x: Two questions: causes? measures? Two separate body paragraphs.
Brainstorm causes: junk food is cheap and advertised, parents are busy, screens, no parks, sugary drinks.
Group them into 2 main causes: diet and activity.
Matching solutions: diet > sugar tax, advertising limits, school lunches; activity > daily PE, walking, screen limits.
Divide the solutions by 'who': governments/schools (Body 2) and families (Body 3).
Example: the UK sugar tax of 2018.
There are many causes of this problem which I will discuss.
The two main causes are changes in diet and a decline in physical activity.
Firstly, children eat too much junk food.
Fast food, sugary soft drinks and packaged snacks are cheap and heavily advertised.
Government should take steps.
Governments could introduce a tax on sugary drinks, as the UK did in 2018.

The number of overweight children has risen in many countries over the past few decades, and the problem now affects developing nations as well as wealthy ones. The two main causes are changes in diet and a decline in physical activity, and both governments and families can take action to reverse the trend.

The first cause is the food children eat. Fast food, sugary soft drinks and packaged snacks are cheap, available on almost every street corner and heavily advertised on television and social media. Many parents work long hours and have little time to cook, so ready-made meals high in fat and salt have replaced home cooking in many households. The second cause is a lack of exercise. Children who once played outside after school now spend hours on phones, tablets and games consoles, and in crowded cities there are often few safe parks where they could be active.

Several measures could help. Governments could introduce a tax on sugary drinks, as the UK did in 2018, a step that led many manufacturers to cut the sugar content of their products. They could also restrict junk food advertising during children's programmes and require schools to serve healthier lunches. Schools themselves should make physical education a daily activity rather than an occasional lesson.

Families have an equally important part to play. Parents can limit screen time, keep fewer sweets and fizzy drinks at home and encourage children to walk or cycle short distances instead of being driven. Above all, they can set an example, since children tend to copy the eating and exercise habits they see at home.

In short, childhood obesity results mainly from unhealthy food and inactive lifestyles. Tackling it requires both public policy, such as taxes and school programmes, and changes in the daily habits of individual families.
notes: The introduction previews the two causes (diet, activity) and the two groups who can act (governments, families). The reader has a map of the essay from the start.
The cause paragraph divides clearly with 'The first cause... The second cause...', and each cause has a why (cheap, advertised, parents busy).
The solutions match the causes directly: diet > sugar tax, advertising limits, school lunches; activity > daily PE, walking. This gives strong coherence.
A real example: the UK sugar tax of 2018 and its result. The example does more than name something. It also says what happened.
The solution paragraph is divided by 'who does what' (governments, schools, families). This is logical and easy to follow.

blocks.x: This prompt does not ask for solutions. It asks for effects, and specifically effects 'on the countryside'. Any words spent on solutions are wasted, because they are not part of the question.

In many developing countries, large numbers of young people are leaving rural areas to live and work in cities.

What are the causes of this trend, and what effects does it have on the countryside?

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

Write at least 250 words.

x: Causes (push): low farm income, unpredictable weather
Causes (pull): factory and service jobs, colleges, hospitals, electricity
Effects on countryside: loss of young workers, farming harder, services close, cycle of leaving
Positive effect: remittances fund education, housing, small businesses
Example: Bangladesh garment industry around Dhaka and Chattogram

Across much of Asia and Africa, young people are leaving villages for cities in large numbers. This movement is driven mainly by the search for work and better services, and it is having serious effects on the rural communities left behind.

The most important cause is employment. Farm incomes are often low and depend on unpredictable weather, while cities offer jobs in factories, construction and services that pay regular wages. In Bangladesh, for example, the garment industry around Dhaka and Chattogram employs around four million people, many of whom have moved from rural districts. Education is a second reason. Most good colleges and universities are in cities, so ambitious students move there to study and often stay after graduating. Cities also offer better hospitals, a steady electricity supply and faster internet, which make urban life more attractive.

The effects on the countryside are significant. First, villages lose their youngest and most energetic workers, leaving mainly older people and children behind. This makes farming harder, and in some areas land is left unused or rented out. Second, local services decline. When the population falls, schools, shops and clinics may close because they no longer have enough users, which in turn pushes even more families to leave.

Not all the effects are negative, however. Many migrants send part of their wages home, and this money helps their families pay for education, healthcare and better housing. In some villages, these payments have also funded small businesses such as shops or poultry farms.

Taken together, the search for work, education and better services is pulling young people into cities. While the money they send home brings some benefits, rural areas are left with ageing populations and weakening services, which may make the trend even harder to reverse.
notes: The prompt says 'effects on the countryside', not effects on the city. Every effect in the essay is about villages. This focus is what TR 8 requires.
The cause paragraph covers both push factors (low farm income, weather) and pull factors (jobs, colleges, hospitals), with the example of the Bangladesh garment industry.
The effect paragraph shows a cycle: the population falls > services close > more families leave. The phrase 'which in turn' links the steps.
A positive effect (remittances) gets one paragraph. This stops the essay from being one-sided and gives a full answer to a question that asks about 'effects' in the plural.
The conclusion adds no new information, but it does offer a final insight ('harder to reverse') that grows out of the cycle described in the body.

blocks.x: The idea of 'push and pull' factors is useful for any prompt on migration, brain drain or urbanisation. Push = the reasons people leave a place. Pull = the reasons they move to a new one.

blocks.x: Here is a typical band 6 answer to the obesity prompt. Both parts are covered, so it is not band 5, but the solutions are vague and the ideas are not developed.

x: Nowadays obesity is a big problem for children in many countries. Many children are becoming fat day by day. There are many causes of this problem and there are also some solutions which I will discuss in this essay.

There are many causes of children obesity. Firstly, children eat too much junk food like burger, pizza and fried chicken. These foods are very tasty but they are not healthy. Many children also drink soft drinks every day instead of water. Secondly, children do not do exercise. They play games in mobile phone and computer all day. They do not go to the field for playing. Thirdly, parents are very busy and they cannot take care of their children properly.

There are some solutions of this problem. Firstly, government should take steps to solve this problem. Government should make some rules for the fast food shops. Secondly, schools should give more importance to sports. Every school should have a playground for the students. Students should play at least one hour every day in school. Thirdly, parents should give healthy food to their children and they should control the mobile phone use of their children.

If we can follow these solutions, then the obesity of children will be reduced. Also, children will be healthy and they will be able to study well. Healthy children are the future of the country. So everyone should be aware about this problem.
In the end, children obesity is a serious problem in the world. The main causes are junk food and less exercise. Government, schools and parents should work together to solve this problem.
notes: TR 6: both causes and solutions are there, so the task is 'addressed', but a solution such as 'Government should make some rules' is vague. What rules? How would they work?
Development: each point is only one or two lines. The cause 'parents are very busy' is never linked to obesity (busy > no cooking > ready meals).
CC 6: both paragraphs use Firstly/Secondly/Thirdly, which is mechanical. P4 is extra, and 'Healthy children are the future of the country' adds nothing.
LR 6: 'children obesity' (should be 'childhood obesity'), 'give importance', 'aware about', 'becoming fat'. The tone is informal and the collocations are wrong.
GRA 6: 'solutions of this problem', 'in mobile phone', 'for playing'. The sentences are mostly simple, with few complex structures.

title: Two-part (direct) questions
bn: Two questions, two direct answers
goal: In this chapter you will learn to separate each part of a two-part question, give each part equal weight, and write a band 8 essay.

blocks.x: In a two-part (direct) question, the prompt describes a situation and then asks two separate questions. The pair can be any combination: why + positive/negative, why + will it continue, what + should. **Each question needs its own direct answer**.

head: Common pair
Example wording
rows: 'Why is this the case? Is this a positive or negative development?'
'Why is this? Do you think cinemas will disappear?'
'Why do fewer people vote? How can this be changed?'
'What is the value of studying history? Should it be compulsory?'
'Who should pay for museums: visitors or the government? Why?'

blocks.x: One advantage of this type is that the prompt gives you the structure. Question 1 = Body 1, Question 2 = Body 2 (or Bodies 2 and 3). You cannot skip either question.
'Positive or negative development?' requires an opinion. Even if you say 'it depends', finish by saying which way it leans.

Treating the two questions as one. For example, in 'Why do people shop online? Is it positive?', writing positives in Body 1 does not answer 'why', because a reason and a benefit are different things.

head: Paragraph
Job
Words
rows: Paraphrase the situation + a short answer to each question, one line each
A full answer to Question 1: 2 reasons, explained, with an example
Question 2: (short) the other side or a concession
Question 2: your main answer, explained, example
Both answers again, in new words

blocks.x: In this type, the introduction matters most. A strong pattern: 'This is mainly because X and Y, and I believe it is a [positive/negative] development.' It answers both questions in one sentence.

x: Q1 'Why': reasons and causes (why it is happening)
Q2 'Positive or negative': judgement + reasons
Q2 'Will X disappear/continue': prediction + reasons, hedging language ('likely', 'may')
Q2 'How can this be changed': solutions (who, what, how)
Q2 'Should X be compulsory': opinion + reasons

Brainstorm 2 points + 1 example for each.
Write both answers in one line in the introduction, then write the body.

blocks.x:
Many people today spend a large amount of their free time on social media.

Why is this the case? Is this a positive or negative development?

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

Write at least 250 words.

x: Question 1 = why (reasons). Question 2 = positive or negative (judgement).
Why brainstorm: endless feeds, recommendation algorithms, likes/notifications, friends share online, students far from home.
Group: (1) design of apps, (2) social need.
Positive or negative: positives (contact, communities, learning, small business); negatives (time lost, self-esteem, anxiety, false news). Judgement: negative.
Order: Body 1 why, Body 2 short positives, Body 3 negatives + judgement.
In this essay I will explain why people use social media so much and whether it is positive or negative.
I believe this happens mainly because the platforms are designed to hold attention and because they meet a real need for connection, but that the overall effect of such heavy use is negative.
Firstly, it is very entertaining.
Feeds never end, and recommendation systems learn what each user likes and keep showing more of it.
It depends on how people use it.
Nevertheless, I consider the development largely negative.

For many people, checking social media is the first thing they do in the morning and the last thing they do at night. I believe this happens mainly because the platforms are designed to hold attention and because they meet a real need for connection, but that the overall effect of such heavy use is negative.

One reason is the way these apps are built. Feeds on Facebook, Instagram and TikTok never end, and their recommendation systems learn what each user likes and keep showing more of it. Likes, comments and notifications give small rewards that make people want to check again and again. Another reason is social. Friends and relatives now share news, photos and invitations mainly online, so people who stay away may feel left out. For students living far from home, social media is also the easiest way to stay in touch with family.

This trend does have some benefits. Social media helps people keep in contact over long distances, find communities with shared interests and learn from free educational content. Small businesses also use it to reach customers at very little cost.

Nevertheless, I consider the development largely negative. Hours spent scrolling are hours taken away from sleep, exercise, reading and face-to-face conversation. Constant comparison with the carefully edited lives of others can lower self-esteem, particularly among teenagers, and research has linked heavy use with anxiety and poor sleep. False news also spreads quickly on these platforms, as users tend to share dramatic posts before checking whether they are true.

Social media is popular because it is designed to be hard to put down and because it meets a genuine need for contact. However, when it fills most of a person's free time, the harm to health, relationships and access to reliable information outweighs its advantages.
notes: The introduction gives a short answer to both questions: why (designed to hold attention, need for connection) and positive/negative (negative). The examiner can see the task coverage at a glance.
Body 1 = question 1 (why), Bodies 2-3 = question 2 (positive or negative). It is clear which question each paragraph answers.
The 'why' paragraph gives two reasons (design, social), and explains the mechanism behind each: 'recommendation systems learn what each user likes'.
Before the negative judgement, a short paragraph accepts the positives. Then 'Nevertheless' introduces the judgement. This is balanced but clear.
The conclusion restates the answers directly, without signpost phrases, and covers both questions. There are no new ideas.

blocks.x:
Nowadays, many people prefer to watch films at home rather than go to the cinema.

Why is this? Do you think cinemas will disappear in the future?

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

Write at least 250 words.

x: Q1 why: cost and convenience; better home equipment; short release window
Q2 prediction: will not disappear; social event; big-screen films (IMAX)
Nuance: fewer, more premium cinemas
Example: multiplexes in Bangladesh malls vs closing single-screen halls

Streaming services have changed how people watch films, and for many households the sofa has replaced the cinema seat. There are clear practical reasons for this shift, but I do not believe cinemas will disappear, although they are likely to become fewer and more specialised.

The main reasons people watch at home are convenience and cost. A monthly subscription to a service such as Netflix often costs less than cinema tickets for a whole family, and it offers thousands of titles that can be paused, rewatched or viewed on a phone. Home equipment has also improved greatly: large flat-screen televisions and sound bars are now affordable, so the gap in quality between home and cinema is far smaller than it was twenty years ago. In addition, many new films appear on streaming platforms only weeks after their cinema release, so there is little reason to hurry.

Even so, I think cinemas will survive, for two reasons. First, going to the cinema is a social event rather than just a way of seeing a story. Friends and couples go out together, and audiences enjoy laughing or gasping as a group. Second, some films are made for a huge screen. Big releases such as superhero films or space dramas still draw large crowds, and formats like IMAX offer an experience that no living room can copy.

What is more likely is that the industry will change shape. Smaller cinemas showing ordinary films may close, while the survivors offer premium seats, food and special events to justify higher prices. In Bangladesh, for instance, multiplex cinemas in shopping malls have expanded even as many older single-screen halls have shut down.

In short, people watch films at home because it is cheaper, easier and increasingly high in quality. Cinemas will lose some customers, but as places for shared experiences and spectacular films, they are unlikely to vanish completely.
notes: The second question is a prediction ('Will cinemas disappear?'). The introduction answers it directly: 'I do not believe cinemas will disappear', with one qualification: 'fewer and more specialised'.
The 'why' paragraph gives 3 reasons (cost/convenience, home equipment, short release window), each with detail. This is a full, developed answer.
The prediction paragraph gives two reasons with 'First... Second...', each with an example (IMAX, superhero films).
The local example in P4 (multiplexes vs single-screen halls in Bangladesh) gives the prediction real-world proof.
Hedging language: 'likely to', 'may close', 'unlikely to vanish'. Being careful rather than certain about the future is a sign of band 8.

blocks.x: In a prediction question, do not say 'will 100%'. Use hedging. It shows grammatical range and makes your logic realistic.

blocks.x: Here is a typical band 6 answer to the social media prompt. It touches on both questions, but the answer to the second question is not clear.

x: In this generation, social media has become a part of our daily life. Many people spend their free time on Facebook, YouTube and TikTok. In this essay I will explain why people use social media so much and whether it is positive or negative.

There are many reasons why people use social media. Firstly, it is very entertaining. People can watch funny videos and see the photos of their friends. Secondly, it is free and easy to use. Anyone can open an account and use it from mobile phone. Thirdly, people can communicate with their friends and relatives who live in other countries. Fourthly, people feel bored in their free time, so they open social media.

Social media has many positive sides. People can get news very quickly from social media. Students can learn many things from YouTube. Also, businessman can sell their products on Facebook. It helps people to connect with each other.

But social media has also negative sides. People waste a lot of time on social media and they cannot concentrate on their study or work. Also, there are many fake news on social media which can create problems in society. Young people become addicted to social media and it is harmful for their health and their eyes. Some people also share private information which is dangerous.

So, social media has both positive and negative sides. It depends on how people use it. If people use it properly, it will be positive, but if they use it too much, it will be negative. So we should use social media carefully.
notes: TR 6: the 'why' part is answered, but the answer to 'positive or negative' is 'it depends'. There is no clear answer to the second question, which is the main reason for band 6.
The reasons are listed (entertaining, free, communicate), but the essay never explains why people spend so much time on it. Even if it is 'free and easy', why do people give it 5 hours?
'In this essay I will explain...' and 'So, ... both positive and negative sides': both lines use up words and give no information.
LR 6: 'In this generation', 'positive sides', 'businessman can sell' (plural/article), 'many fake news' (uncountable). Repetition: 'social media' appears in almost every line.
CC: the paragraphs are logical, so it does not fall below 6. But 'Firstly, Secondly, Thirdly, Fourthly, Also, But' is all mechanical.

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

Write at least 250 words.

x: Type: Discuss both views | Topic: Media
View A (newspapers): edited and checked; deeper analysis; less fake news.
View B (internet): instant, free, many sources, video and live updates.

Example: fake stories spreading on social media vs corrections in a newspaper.

International brands and products are now sold in almost every country. Do the advantages of this outweigh the disadvantages?

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

Write at least 250 words.

x: Type: Advantages/disadvantages (outweigh) | Topic: Globalisation
Thesis: Advantages outweigh.
Advantages: more choice, better quality, jobs in factories and shops, lower prices through competition.
Disadvantages: local businesses close, cultures look the same everywhere.
Weighing: local firms can compete by improving; consumers benefit every day.
Example: Bangladeshi garment exports to global brands; local fast food chains copying global ones.

blocks.x:

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

Write at least 250 words.

x: Type: Advantages/disadvantages (outweigh) | Topic: Government and society
Thesis: Disadvantages outweigh, unless governments plan ahead.
Advantages: experience in work and volunteering; grandparents help with childcare.
Disadvantages: higher pension and health costs; fewer workers paying tax.
Weighing: costs grow every year, benefits cannot balance them without reform.
Example: Japan, where more than a quarter of people are over 65.

Advantages: work experience, money saved, maturity, clearer choice of subject.
Disadvantages: lose study habits, start career a year later, travel is costly.

Advantages: children cared for by trusted family; free compared with day care; children learn family values and stories.

pages.h: Problem, solution, cause and effect prompts (13-16)

blocks.x:

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

Cause 1: cheap single-use plastic everywhere (bags, bottles, packaging).
Cause 2: poor waste collection and recycling, especially in fast-growing cities.
Solution 1 (matches 1): fees or bans on single-use plastic; England's 5p bag charge cut use by over 80 per cent.

Advertising aimed at children should be banned. To what extent do you agree or disagree?

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

Write at least 250 words.

x: Thesis: Largely agree, especially for unhealthy products; full ban hard to enforce
Body 1: children cannot judge adverts
Body 2: pressure on families; junk food and obesity
Body 3 (concession): online ads hard to control; practical partial ban

Children today see thousands of advertisements a year on television, YouTube and mobile games. Some people believe that all advertising directed at children should be banned. I agree with this view to a large extent, particularly for products that can harm their health, although a complete ban would be difficult to enforce.

The main argument for a ban is that young children cannot judge advertisements critically. Many children under about eight cannot reliably tell the difference between an advert and an ordinary programme, and even older children rarely understand that an advert is designed to persuade them. When cartoon characters promote sugary cereals or expensive toys, children simply believe what they see. It seems unfair for companies with large marketing budgets to target an audience that cannot defend itself.

Advertising aimed at children also creates problems for families. Children who want the latest toy or snack often put pressure on their parents, and this can cause arguments at home and push low-income families to spend money they cannot afford. Adverts for junk food are especially harmful, since they encourage eating habits that contribute to childhood obesity.

However, banning every advert would not be simple. Children now spend much of their time online, where advertising is mixed with entertainment through influencers and sponsored videos, which are hard to regulate. Some adverts, such as those for books or road safety campaigns, may even be useful. A more practical approach might be strict bans on unhealthy food advertising and on adverts during children's programmes, together with clear labelling of sponsored content.

For these reasons, I largely support restricting advertising aimed at children, as they are easily influenced and the effects on health and family budgets can be serious. Governments should start with the most harmful products and extend the rules to online platforms over time.
notes: 'To a large extent' + 'particularly for...' + 'although...': one sentence makes the position, the focus and the limit all clear.
The main idea of Body 1 (children cannot judge adverts) is supported by an age-specific detail (under about eight).
Body 2 has an effect chain: adverts > pressure on parents > arguments and overspending; junk food ads > obesity.
The concession paragraph offers a practical solution ('strict bans on unhealthy food advertising'), which makes the 'largely agree' position logical.
Topic vocabulary: 'marketing budgets', 'sponsored content', 'influencers', 'regulate'. All of these are natural collocations.

blocks.q: Rewrite the thesis of this essay so that it completely disagrees.
blocks.a: 'I disagree. Parents, not governments, should decide what their children watch, and a total ban would also end useful adverts for books and safety campaigns.'

pages.h: Practice 22: model essay (discuss both views, culture)

blocks.x:
Some people think that international tourism damages local cultures, while others believe it helps to protect them. Discuss both these views and give your own opinion.

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

Write at least 250 words.

x: View A: customs changed for visitors; residents pushed out (Venice)
View B: money for heritage and crafts (Paharpur)
My view: B, if tourism is managed

Mass tourism brings millions of visitors to historic towns and traditional communities every year. Some argue that this contact slowly destroys local culture, while others believe tourist money helps to keep traditions alive. In my opinion, tourism can do both, but when it is sensibly managed, its protective effect is stronger.

Those who see tourism as harmful point out that local customs are often changed to suit visitors. Traditional dances may be cut into short performances for hotel guests, and handmade crafts may be replaced by cheap souvenirs made in factories. In popular destinations such as Venice, rising rents and crowds have pushed many residents out of the historic centre, so the places tourists come to see gradually lose the people who gave them their character.

Supporters of tourism, on the other hand, argue that it gives communities a financial reason to protect their heritage. Entrance fees help to pay for the repair of temples, palaces and museums, and visitors who buy local crafts allow artisans to keep practising skills that might otherwise disappear. In Bangladesh, for example, visitors to the ancient Buddhist monastery at Paharpur bring income to nearby villages and draw attention to the need to preserve the site.

I find the second view more convincing, provided tourism is properly controlled. Limits on visitor numbers, rules on building near heritage sites and support for genuine local businesses can reduce the damage while keeping the income. Without tourism, many small communities would have neither the money nor the motivation to protect their traditions.

To my mind, tourism is not in itself a threat to local culture. When it is well managed, it gives people both the means and the reason to preserve the customs and places that make their communities distinctive.
notes: The introduction gives a mixed opinion, but with a clear direction: 'its protective effect is stronger', plus a condition: 'when it is sensibly managed'.
Both views have a real example: Venice (residents pushed out) and Paharpur (income for villages). One is global and one is local.
'Those who see tourism as harmful', 'Supporters of tourism': this is distancing language, so the opinion stays separate from the views.
The opinion paragraph makes the condition specific: visitor limits, building rules, local businesses.
In the conclusion, the phrase 'means and reason' brings together the two ideas from the body (money, motivation).

blocks.x: Mixing one global example with one local (Bangladesh) example makes the essay feel both specific and personal.

pages.h: Practice 23: model essay (problem and solution, technology and work)

blocks.x:
Artificial intelligence is increasingly being used to do jobs that were previously done by people. What problems might this cause, and what can be done to reduce them?

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

Write at least 250 words.

x: Problems: job loss, inequality, bias and unclear responsibility
Solutions: retraining, taxes or training budgets from companies, human review of AI decisions
Matching: each solution answers one problem

Artificial intelligence can now write reports, answer customer questions and even help doctors read X-rays. As these systems take over tasks once done by people, several problems are likely to appear, but governments, companies and workers can take steps to reduce them.

The most obvious problem is job loss. Workers in call centres, data entry and basic translation face the greatest risk, because their tasks follow clear patterns that software can copy. Many of these employees cannot easily move into new careers, especially if they are older or have limited education. A second problem is inequality. The profits from automation tend to go to the companies that own the technology and the small number of highly skilled people who build it, while wages for routine work may fall.

There are also concerns about fairness and responsibility. AI systems learn from past data, so they can repeat existing biases, for example by rejecting job applicants from certain backgrounds. When such a system makes a mistake, it is often unclear who should be held responsible: the company, the developer or the user.

Several measures could reduce these problems. Governments could fund retraining programmes so that workers whose jobs are automated can learn new skills, such as checking the output of AI tools, or move into fields like nursing where human contact still matters. Companies that save money through automation could be required to contribute through taxes or training budgets. Finally, laws should require important AI decisions, such as those about hiring or loans, to be explained and reviewed by a human.

In short, the spread of AI at work may lead to job losses, wider inequality and unfair decisions. Retraining, a fairer sharing of the gains and clear rules on responsibility can reduce these risks, so that the technology benefits society as a whole.
notes: The introduction makes the topic real with concrete examples (reports, customer questions, X-rays), then previews both parts of the task.
The problem paragraph uses 'because' to explain why those jobs are at risk: 'tasks follow clear patterns'.
The problems and solutions are matched: job loss > retraining; inequality > taxes/training budgets; bias and responsibility > a human review law.
The modal verbs are precise: 'could fund', 'could be required', 'should require'. Possibility and recommendation are kept apart.
Hedging: 'are likely to appear', 'may fall', 'tend to go'. The tone about future technology is careful and realistic.

blocks.q: In this essay, which solution matches which problem? Write the three pairs.
blocks.a: Job loss > retraining programmes; inequality > companies contribute through taxes or training budgets; bias and responsibility > laws requiring human review of AI decisions.
